News.title: Chilling moment knife fight breaks out on busy bus with huge blades as passengers left terrified
News.content:
SWORD THUGS Chilling moment knife fight breaks out on busy bus with huge blades as passengers left terrified







Next

THIS is the terrifying moment a knife fight breaks out on a busy bus armed with huge blades, as passengers are left terrified.

Footage of the brawl shows the violence erupting in the middle of the stationary bus while onlookers are caught up in the ordeal.



The violent outbreak is thought to be linked to an ongoing police investigation following a stabbing in Birmingham this week.

As the footage begins, a man can be seen standing on the Arriva vehicle, just past the driver’s cab area.



He appears to brandish a long knife in one hand while looking at a group of around four youths outside the bus as he yells to the driver: “Go, go, go.”

The bus driver though doesn’t start off and the group outside the vehicle continue yelling while another bangs repeatedly on the window.



Just moments later, a fight breaks out with weapons, including a knife and a black metallic object.

An onlooker can be heard shouting: “He’s got a knife you know.”



A number of distressed passengers try to get up from their seats and leave, including an elderly lady, but can’t as the melee unfolds.

A youth appears to hit out several times, armed with a blade, before seemingly stamping on someone lying on the ground, as others rush to join in.

The shocking clip comes to an end as onlookers call for someone to call the police.



On Tuesday evening a man was stabbed in the centre of Birmingham and left with serious injuries which cops said are “likely to be life-changing”.

A man was chased onto a bus in Corporation Street by a group at around 10.30pm, according to West Midlands Police.

Dello Alphaoumar, 21, has been charged with violent disorder and a 17-year-old boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, has been charged with violent disorder, threatening a person with a blade, and possession of a hammer.

A second boy aged 16 has been released on bail.

Cops are still looking for a fourth suspect in connection with the attack and have appealed for any witnesses or anyone with footage of what happened to contact them.



Members of the public should get in touch by calling 101 or using the force’s live chat on their website, quoting log 5780 of October 13.

News.title: Britain faces ‘frank conversation’ about need to prepare for war, warns Army chief
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN will soon face a “frank conversation” about the need to prepare for war, the Army chief has warned.

General Sir Roly Walker told troops: “You didn’t know this, but our nation is going to need you.”



The former SAS officer said the government would try and explain the people would have to make sacrifices “to prioritise defence and security”.

The Chief of the General Staff had previously warned that 2027 was a year of peak risk for Britain with “just enough time to prepare”.



Speaking to 700 soldiers from the Army’s high readiness global response force he said: “There was a time that our nation didn’t want to think of a time when it would need its soldiers to fight in a war.

“But…there is extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment.”



In comments recorded by Forces News he added: “Very soon the political leaders of this country will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country, about just what is going on and where the risk lies, and what the nation must need to be prepared to do.”

He said Labour would “try and explain” that citizens have to make sacrifices “to prioritise defence and security”.

But Labour has repeatedly refused to slash welfare to fund the armed forces.

Gen Walker told soldiers at Catterick Garrison, North Yorkshire, that the “burden of fighting” was placed squarely on the soldiers of the most inexperienced and junior soldiers.



He added: “And I’m looking at you because it’s on you that the defence of this nation will rest, if ultimately, you are called to fight.”

News.title: Burnham must fix the many real problems Britain has – not open an insane Brexit can of worms
News.content:
No gift of gob







Next

ANDY Burnham visited Scotland yesterday embroiled in a row with the SNP over a second independence referendum.

The PM found himself in this mess because of his worrying compulsion to speak first, think later.



Indeed, in the last few weeks alone, he has suffered multiple bouts of foot-in-mouth.

There was his catastrophically ill-judged intervention into the Manchester City financial doping scandal.



His false claim that Russia had helped swing the outcome of the Brexit referendum.

And his suggestion in the Commons that another IndyRef was possible — thereby giving fresh impetus to the SNP’s mania to smash up the UK.



Yesterday, he tried to mop up after himself by categorically ruling out another Indy vote.

Constitutional issues, he rightly said, waste “too much time, consume too much energy”.

So let’s hope he now follows his own logic and stops his divisive bid to refight the Brexit battle.

No one should want to bog Britain down again in the misery of the Brexit wars.



Burnham is cynically trying to lure back diehard Europhiles who fled Labour.

But, deep down, he must surely know rejoining the EU is a can of worms it would be insane to open.

Fix the many real problems that Britain has – not those which only exist in the minds of deranged Remainers.

Evil out early

THE impending release from prison of the mother of Henry Nowak’s murderer is not just soft justice. It’s no justice.

Devious Kiran Kaur was jailed for concealing the dagger her son Vickrum Digwa used to cold-bloodedly kill the innocent 18-year-old student.



Her duplicity played a part in the police wrongly arresting Henry even as he lay dying in the street.

Yet thanks to the Labour Government’s shameful scheme to free thousands of lags early, she’ll be let out this year after serving just a THIRD of her three-year term.

Kaur, an Indian national, has been warned she could be deported.

If immigration officials manage to get her on a plane, then good riddance.

But she must first serve a sentence befitting her evil crime.



Final nail

DIY SOS has been a much-loved show since first airing 27 years ago.

Nick Knowles and his team transforming the homes of families hit by hard luck is the sort of broadcasting viewers expect in return for being forced to pay a licence fee.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

So it’s a huge mistake to bin it for being “too expensive”.

If the Beeb wants to cut costs, it should slash woke nonentities nobody outside its own bloated management ever asked for?

News.title: Beware the Burnhamwave! Sky-high migration levels have put a time-bomb under UK’s finances… now Labour could detonate it
News.content:
Next

HAS a Prime Minister ever followed a policy so brazenly the opposite of that which voters thought they were electing him for?

As we trooped to the polling stations in December 2019, the words “take back control” were still ringing in our ears.



We assumed that Boris Johnson meant to apply this to UK migration policy more than anything else.

Yet the result was almost a ­complete loss of control.



The statistics of the so-called “Boris-wave” make for astonishing reading.

In the 12 months to June 2021, a net 251,000 migrants arrived in ­Britain. The following year, it ­ballooned to 681,000, then 924,000 in 2023, before falling back to 649,000 in the year to June 2024 as Rishi Sunak finally began to get a grip.

In Sunak’s last year in office, the salary threshold for a skilled worker visa rose sharply, while overseas students and care workers were banned in most cases from bringing dependents with them to Britain.

By that time, however, a net 2.5million migrants had arrived in four years — equivalent to 3.7 per cent of the UK population.



Of these, 171,000 were illegal migrants, of whom around four-fifths arrived on small boats.

We know about the difficulties that governments have with human rights lawyers when trying to return illegal migrants. But, markedly, the vast majority of migrants who arrived in the Boriswave were perfectly legal: The Home Office invited them in.

While net migration figures have continued to fall, to 204,000 in the 12 months to June 2025 and 171,000 in the 12 months to December 2025, a time bomb now sits below the UK’s public finances.

It is primed to explode when the Boriswave migrants are free to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain, which in most cases will be five years after they first came here.

At that point, they could be transformed from workers, students and asylum-seekers on temporary visas into permanent residents eligible for benefits, including the state pension.



Until recently, it looked as if the current government was aware of the problem and was committed to ­keeping the numbers low.

Home Secretary Shabana ­Mahmood seemed to understand that ­such levels of net migration are unsustainable from an economic and social perspective.

She proposed to double the period required to apply for ILR to ten years in most cases. For low-skilled workers, such as care workers, it would be up to 15 years.



And in all cases, it would become dependent on applicants demonstrating their commitment to Britain.

They would have to show that they had been supporting themselves financially and paying their taxes.

And they would have to have high proficiency in the English language and no criminal record.

In addition, in March, Mahmood applied a “visa brake”, denying visas to nationals from four countries who stand accused of exploiting our ­system of legal migration in order to claim asylum in Britain: Namely Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan.

Like other ministers who have ­proposed ways of saving the taxpayer money, however, Mahmood has run into a seemingly insurmountable obstacle: Backbench Labour MPs, who have threatened to rebel against the plans.



For many of them, it seems a straightforward knee-jerk reaction.

They could never, ever bring ­themselves to vote for measures which toughen the migration system because they think it would make them “bad people”.

And besides, they argue, Britain needs people such as care workers (although clearly any care worker who wins ILR immediately has no obligation to stay in that role). Worryingly, PM Andy Burnham seems to sympathise.

Mahmood has already tried to appease Labour hardliners by ­promising legal routes for refugees.

Then, at last month’s Labour Party Conference, she declared she was open to watering down her reforms in reaction to some of her colleagues describing the proposals as “unfair”.



It seems likely that her reforms could go the same way as Keir Starmer’s attempts to hold back the runaway budget for Personal ­Independence Payments, or PIP.

Initially, those reforms were supposed to save the taxpayer a modest £5billion a year, but were abandoned after enough backbench Labour MPs threatened to rebel in order to threaten Starmer’s enormous majority. For him, it was the beginning of the end.

Until recently, the pro-migration lobby liked to try to argue that migration was a non-problem because migrants helped boost the economy and make us all richer. But that myth has been shattered in recent times following revelations about just how many migrants are living on benefits.



This week, the Centre For Social Justice revealed that there are 1.3million non-UK nationals receiving Universal Credit, an increase of 38 per cent in the past four years.

Including the state pension, there are 1.85million non-UK nationals on benefits, costing the taxpayer £23billion a year.

The bill, says the CSJ, is projected to rise to £27billion by 2030. It is true that certain industries have become reliant on migrant workers. Figures produced this week, also by the CSJ, show that only one in five new payrolled positions created since 2014 — 734,000 out of 3.7million — were filled by a UK national.

But the idea that all migrants are beavering away to boost the ­economy is a fallacy.

In 2023, when net migration was nearly one million, just 66,000 of the arrivals came on skilled worker visas, bringing 52,200 dependents with them. Another 145,800 came on health and social care visas, who between them brought 202,800 dependents. The single largest groups were those who came on study visas, accounting for 456,700.



Overseas students are, in effect, an export industry — they earn the country money — but they also come with a cost. They, and the 143,300 dependents they brought with them, put extra pressure on public services.

There is also a big problem with people coming to Britain allegedly to study, but then dropping out of their courses and becoming illegal migrants.

In theory, since September last year universities have been banned from taking in overseas students if fewer than 95 per cent of those offered places actually turn up to enrol, or if fewer than 90 per cent complete their courses.

Had these rules been in place in 2022, 22 universities would have fallen foul of them.

Finally, 2023 saw 80,100 overseas nationals granted family visas to come to Britain. And 68,500 were allowed to stay on humanitarian grounds, including asylum-seekers.



A further 40,300 Ukrainians arrived thanks to visa arrangements made especially for them.

The Office for Budgetary Responsibility has become more open about just how much migrants end up costing the UK taxpayer. Low-skilled migrants start costing the country from day one, as the benefits they are paid and the cost of the public services they use grow to exceed tax revenues.

By the time they reach retirement age — currently 66 — a low-skilled migrant will have cost Britain a net £150,000. If they stay in the country to collect their pension and live to the age of 80, a single, low-skilled migrant will have cost the taxpayer £500,000.

Initially, a migrant on the average wage will produce a ­positive return for the taxpayer. By the age of 66 they will have seemingly contributed a net £722,000. But that falls away when they stop earning and start claiming their state pension.

If they live to the age of 92, they will end up costing the taxpayer.



Only high-wage migrants are guaranteed to end up making a positive contribution to the public purse.

As Sir David Miles, an economics professor who serves as an ­executive member of the OBR, wrote in an essay last year, trying to rely on migrants to mend the public finances is futile because they bring with them an ever- expanding bill for public services.

It also costs the taxpayer twice over: Once to pay for the public services used by, and benefits claimed by, the migrants; and again to pay for the benefits claimed by UK citizens who have lost out in the jobs market to migrants and end up on jobless benefits instead.

Mahmood is going to have to decide which way she wants to nod: To economists like Miles, who warn that high levels of migration are leading us to fiscal disaster.

Or to emotional Labour MPs who have fooled themselves into ­thinking that mass migration is the mark of a civilised country.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

There is no guarantee she will turn the right way.

The Boriswave is about to turn into the Burnhamwave.

News.title: Fury as Czech PM says he wants  Britain to rejoin the EU so he can have more of our cash
News.content:
Next

THE Czech PM says he wants Britain to rejoin the EU — so he can have more of our cash.

Asked if he would support the UK’s return to the bloc, Czech PM Andrej Babis replied: “Yes of course. We need more money.”



He was quizzed on Sky News after PM Andy Burnham opened the door to reversing Brexit by putting a rejoin pledge in Labour’s next manifesto.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said last night: “The EU’s mask has dropped.



“They want us to rejoin so they can take our money and spend it on projects Brits will never see.”

Ex-Tory MP Sir Simon Clarke accused Mr Babis of “saying the quiet bit out loud”.



He added: “If we were to return to the EU, we wouldn’t have our rebate, so we’d be shouldering even more of a disproportionate burden to subsidise the poorer parts of Europe.”

In 2020, the final year of UK membership in the EU, Britain’s net contribution was £12.6billion — one of the largest in the bloc.

Mr Burnham used his conference speech last month to vow closer ties with the EU in the name of economic growth.

He has refused to rule out campaigning to rejoin the bloc entirely after saying Brexit has “done more harm than good.”

News.title: Moment cops find £12,000 worth of lingerie and sex toys in car after thieves break into Ann Summers store
News.content:
Next

THIS is the startling moment cops find £12,000 worth of lingerie and sex toys in the boot of a car after thieves raid an Ann Summers store.

Police can be seen stuffing racy bras and other items of clothing into large bags which will later be used as evidence.



As more and more items are taken from the back of the vehicle a stash of boxed-up sex toys are also removed.

Jason Kamal, 48, and Ashley Hillsley, 21, smashed their way into the branch in Long Row, Nottingham, during the early hours of August 14.



The pair, both wearing gloves and hi-visibility clothing, ripped an alarm panel from the wall and damaged a stockroom door before transferring £12,059 of goods, including negligees and sex toys, into a vehicle.

Police raced to the scene after reports of a burglary in progress at 4.32am and arrived within three minutes, forcing the pair to flee on foot.

Officers detained both men and body-cam footage shows them discovering a huge stash of Ann Summers stock in the boot of Hillsley’s car.

The footage, released by Nottinghamshire Police, begins as a cop gets out of his vehicle to give chase as one of the robbers legs it down the street.



Shouts of “stop” can be heard.

As Kamal realises the game is up, he complies with the policeman’s instructions.

The thief is wearing a grey t-shirt, blue sweatpants and a yellow hi-visibility jacket.

He takes off his black backpack before following orders to get down on his knees.



As he removes his jacket he’s told to put his hands on his head.

He’s told not to move as the handcuffs go on and he’s told his rights.

A policewoman is seen searching through his backpack.

The clip then switches to the actual raid and a man is seen searching around a back office.



Later, a man is seen walking down the stairs at the back of the building, carrying a large box.

Shortly after, a second man appears, also carrying a large box.

The footage ends with police searching through the boot of a blue car and removing potential evidence.

Kamal initially denied entering Ann Summers despite his face being visible on CCTV.

Hillsley said he was bullied into the burglary, and his primary role was to be on lookout and assist.



He was told he would receive a large sum of money, and he would no longer be “a nobody.”

Kamal was also arrested on suspicion of another burglary which had occurred at Professional Mobile in Front Street in Arnold on July 28.

Kamal had left a vape at the scene of the crime with his DNA all over it and the phone he was using was one stolen from the store.

During this burglary, Kamal stole a number of electronic devices valued at around £13,000.

Both offenders appeared at Nottingham Crown Court on October 15 for sentencing.



Kamal was given a three-year prison sentence for both burglaries while Hillsley received a community order for the Ann Summers burglary.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The arrests were part of the force’s Operation Reclaim which targets criminals in Nottingham city centre.

Launched in May, it aims to create a hostile environment for criminals to operate.

News.title: Hilarious moment Zelensky responds to Trump question with only a cheeky smile: ‘This is my answer’
News.content:
Next

THIS is the hilarious moment Volodymyr Zelensky smirks when he is asked if Donald Trump is using him as a scapegoat for his own problems.

The Ukrainian president cheekily smiled in response to claims Kyiv is being thrown under the bus to distract from the war in Iran and high energy prices.



Zelensky and Trump’s relationship reached new lows in recent days – with the US leader on Thursday calling him more difficult than Vladimir Putin.

The spiralling row kicked off when Washington and Moscow signed a diesel deal – sparking fury in Ukraine.



Kyiv went on to launch strikes on Russian energy hubs – despite US warnings against such attacks – prompting Trump to call for a new Ukrainian leader.

Asked by a reporter on Friday if Trump is using him as a fall guy, Zelensky simply smirked before receiving a round of laughter from the crowd.



He then said: “This is my answer.”

The Kyiv-Washington dispute has led to the US cutting off Ukraine‘s full access to Starlink – Elon Musk‘s satellite-based internet system.

The technology is crucial in helping Ukraine fend off Russian strikes – and Zelensky has said its outage will lead to more civilian deaths.

On Friday, Trump blasted Zelensky as “harder to deal with than Putin” after Ukraine launched another round of strikes on Russian oil depots.



The US president called Kyiv’s latest blitz a “disgrace” as he continued his furious spat with Zelensky just days after being accused of “betraying” Ukraine.

Kyiv targeted Russia with new strikes just hours after Zelensky told Piers Morgan his wartorn country was losing the US to a scheming Putin.

Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s Ryazan region and caused a fire to break out at a major oil refinery.



The attack was the first Ukrainian strike on an energy facility since Trump announced a surprise “energy ceasefire” on Sunday.

Trump, who declared the truce without Kyiv or Moscow formally agreeing to it, fumed at Ukraine for the attacks on Thursday.

Russia’s own overnight strikes killed three innocent civilians with drones in Kharkiv, according to regional governor Oleh Synegubov.



Ukraine’s Volyn region bordering Poland was also plunged into darkness by Moscow overnight as 370,000 people were left without power.

Trump is yet to comment on Russia’s strikes but he did go on to blame Zelensky for driving up global energy prices in a scathing interview.

“Zelensky’s not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump continued.

“He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t. I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.

“As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin. And when you have that kind of hatred, it’s very hard to get something settled.”



The US president then said Zelensky and his cabinet have “destroyed the country”.

It has now been revealed that Ukraine is reportedly running low on US Patriot air-defence missiles.

The defensive weapons are critical for Ukraine to help them fend off ballistic missile attacks.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Ukrainian official told the Washington Post: “As of Oct 7, there were only 10 missiles left.

“These were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining.”

News.title: Cops probe wife of PM’s National Security Adviser after she appears to support banned group Palestine Action
News.content:
TERROR GROUP TWEET Cops probe wife of PM’s National Security Adviser after she appears to support banned group Palestine Action







Next

COPS are probing the wife of the PM’s National Security Adviser after she appeared to support banned group Palestine Action.

Sarah Helm, who is married to No10 aide Jonathan Powell, wrote on X: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”



Scotland Yard said: “We have been made aware of an X post on 15 October referencing Palestine Action.

“It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether further investigation may be required.”



Ms Helm’s post was a reference to Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who claims her books have been withdrawn from UK shops because of her support for Palestine Action.

A Government spokeswoman said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the Government in any capacity.”

Support for Palestine Action became a crime last year.

Ministers said it commits acts of terrorism.



Reform MP Danny Kruger last night wrote to PM Andy Burnham with concerns over Ms Helm’s comments. He said: “As you will know, and as Jonathan Powell will certainly be aware, Palestine Action is a proscribed terrorist organisation under the Terrorism Act 2000.

“It has been an offence for anybody in Britain to display support for this group since July 2025.

“I am concerned that Ms Helm appears to have breached the law and alarmed at what influence, if any, she might have on government policy with respect to Israel/Palestine and to the enforcement of the proscription.

“I would be grateful if you could please write to me outlining your position on this matter together with an explanation of what steps, if any, you believe it would be appropriate for the police to take against Ms Helm.”

News.title: Nurse took £770k from vulnerable 99-year-old and splashed cash on home improvements and campervan
News.content:
Nurse took £770k from vulnerable 99-year-old and splashed cash on home improvements and campervan

A nurse looking after a 99-year-old woman, who had no family, transferred ownership of the pensioner's house to herself and took hundreds of thousands of pounds

View 2 Images Rebecca Burwood took £770k from a vulnerable pensioner while caring for her (Image: Facebook)

A nurse who took £770,000 from a "vulnerable and lonely" 99-year-old woman and spent the cash on vehicles and home improvements has been struck off.

‌



‌



Rebecca Burwood exploited the elderly woman between 2017 and 2023 while working as deputy manager at a care home, a tribunal found. A Nursing and Midwifery Council fitness to practise committee heard Ms Burwood, while working at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, north Wales, used "manipulation and coercion to acquire funds" from the woman.

‌



It was alleged Burwood used some of the money on personal cosmetic surgery while evidence showed some of the cash was spent on "house improvements, utility bills and council tax".

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Burwood has been struck off (Image: Facebook)

Older people urged to get flu jab after data reveals nearly 4,000 deaths from horror winter READ MORE :

Burwood abused her position and became the elderly woman's lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs, on May 5 2018, while overseeing her care at the same time. The nurse allegedly did this without telling anyone else at the care home.

‌



The 99-year-old, who did not have any family, also transferred ownership of her house, valued at £400,000, prior to Burwood entering Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in 2018.

Evidence showed more than £370,000 left the woman’s bank account over five years, including £160,000 in large cash withdrawals from ATMs.

Burwood persuaded the pensioner to pay £20,000 for a car and £9,000 for a campervan, claiming the vehicles would allow them to go on days out together. The pensioner was "vulnerable and lonely" following a fall and relied on Burwood for friendship and social contact, the panel heard.

‌



The committee found the nurse used "emotional blackmail" by telling the elderly woman she would not be able to take her for days out if she did not have access to her money, adding she was "withdrawing large sums of money almost daily" from her bank account.

The pensioner's bank account was subsequently frozen over concerns about spending, but Burwood tried to have the restrictions lifted and took her to a bank branch. Staff at the bank described Burwood as "almost blackmailing" the woman and said she had told the pensioner to ask for the accounts to be unlocked.

This bank referred the situation to North Wales Police, which launched an investigation. The force then took no further action as the woman, who has since died, did not want to make a complaint.

‌



The committee heard the woman regarded Burwood as a friend and believed the nurse had "learned from her mistakes". The pensioner however had told safeguarding staff she was shocked and disappointed by the amount that had been spent from her account.

In written statements to the panel, Burwood said: "I now recognise that, even where a gift is offered voluntarily or with good intentions, as was the case here for me, accepting anything beyond a trivial token can compromise, or appear to compromise, professional judgment.

"(The elderly woman) was not only someone I later encountered in a professional context, but someone I had known for many years and came to see as a dear friend and grandmother-type figure. I had no understanding of the scope of an LPA and now recognise that this was a major failing on my part."

Article continues below

In its ruling, the nursing panel said Burwood's actions were "deplorable and a disgrace to the profession". The committee said although the nurse said the 99-year-old had approved gifting off her assets, this was undermined by evidence demonstrating she was "shocked and disappointed at the amount of money being spent".

It added that it was "improbable" the woman would have "knowingly and willingly given away her home and substantial sums of money leaving her with only a modest amount of cash and the risk of not being able to fund her own care".

News.title: School dinners firm ordered to shut down after 'rodent droppings' discovered in kitchen
News.content:
School dinners firm ordered to shut down after 'rodent droppings' discovered in kitchen

Irish school meals provider The Lunch Bag was served with a closure order after rodent droppings were found on ovens, food-contact materials and inside cupboards

View 2 Images Food packaging and open foodstuffs at The Lunch Bag's premises were 'exposed to contamination by rodents' (file image) (Image: Supplied)

An Irish school meals provider was hit with a closure order after rodent droppings were found on ovens, food-contact materials and inside cupboards.

‌



‌



The Lunch Bag was among 12 food businesses in Ireland served with closure orders in September for breaches of food safety legislation, the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) announced on Thursday.

‌



The closure order, issued by an officer of the Health Service Executive on September 23, stated that rodent droppings were found on the stainless steel rims of ovens, on food-contact materials, on shelving beneath a sink and inside cupboards.

‌



The report also stated that the premises, equipment and bathroom were "not kept clean", with dead insects observed on window ledges and floors.

View 2 Images Pizza Petito was also served with a closure order after inspectors found an 'active infestation of rats in the premises and in particular in the kitchen area' (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The order applies to all areas associated with The Lunch Bag's food business activities at Timahoe GAA, Páirc Mhochua Cremorgan, Timahoe, Portlaoise.

‌



The report concluded: "The above conditions pose a grave and immediate danger to public health. Food packaging and open foodstuffs were stored in the area leaving them exposed to contamination by rodents.

"There is a serious risk of food being contaminated with pathogenic bacteria likely to render the food unfit for human consumption, injurious to health or contaminated in such a way that would be unreasonable to expect it to be consumed in that state."

Nine other closure orders were served under the FSAI Act 1998 on the following businesses:

‌



Furlong's Bar & Lounge and Nellie's Takeaway: Curracloe, Wexford

Curracloe, Wexford Fia's Café: 57 Thomas Street, Prior's Land, Limerick

57 Thomas Street, Prior's Land, Limerick Pizza Petito (Takeaway): 9 Orwell Road, Rathgar, Dublin 6

9 Orwell Road, Rathgar, Dublin 6 Centra (Retailer): Ardlo Manor, Mullagh, Cavan

Ardlo Manor, Mullagh, Cavan Summergrove House (B&B used primarily as a private dwelling): Summergrove, Mountmellick, Co Laois (all areas associated with the food business activities)

Summergrove, Mountmellick, Co Laois (all areas associated with the food business activities) Everest Kitchen Nepalese (Restaurant/Café): The Friary Bow, Abbey Street, Ennis, Clare

The Friary Bow, Abbey Street, Ennis, Clare The Thatch (Restaurant/Café): Killenard, Portarlington, Laois

Killenard, Portarlington, Laois Marka Cadey 2 (Restaurant/Café): 5 Talbot Street, Dublin 1

5 Talbot Street, Dublin 1 The Hopsack (Service Sector): Swan Leisure Centre, Lower Rathmines Road, Rathmines, Dublin 6

Two further closure orders were served under European Union (Official Controls in relation to Food Legislation) Regulations 2020 on the following businesses:

Eskimo Pizza and Indian (Takeaway): Main Street, Ballyheigue, Kerry

Main Street, Ballyheigue, Kerry J2 Sushi & Bento (Restaurant/Café): 75 Main Street, Swords, County Dublin

‌



The closure order for Pizza Petito, which was issued on September 23, stated that there was an "active infestation of rats in the premises and in particular in the kitchen area". The report said rodent droppings were "noted to be spread widely across the kitchen", including beneath a fridge.

Greg Dempsey, chief executive of the FSAI, said on Thursday: "The Closure Orders served in September once again highlight the importance of maintaining robust food safety and hygiene practices across all food businesses.

"Issues such as inadequate pest control, poor cleaning standards and unsafe food storage continue to be the main reasons for enforcement action."

Article continues below

He added: "Food businesses should be continuously improving their food safety standards via regular training, availing of our free online learning portal, as well as promoting a strong culture of food safety within their businesses."

News.title: Hero dad 'traumatised' after stopping mass Oregon school shooter who killed three children and teacher
News.content:
Hero dad 'traumatised' after stopping mass Oregon school shooter who killed three children and teacher

Four people - including three children aged five, eight and 11 - were killed in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Oregon on Thursday

View 3 Images Dad Kaylub Giamanco intervened during the attack and shot the 16-year-old gunman (Image: Handout)

The "heroic" bystander who killed a 16-year-old gunman during a deadly school shooting in Oregon is the dad of two girls who attend the school, it has emerged.

‌



‌



The attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend on Thursday left three children, aged five, eight and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher dead. A seven-year-old pupil and a 54-year-old teacher were critically injured.

‌



Kenda Freeman said on Friday that her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened during Thursday's attack and shot the teenage gunman. "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said in a statement to reporters.

‌



View 3 Images Three children and a teacher were killed in the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School (Image: AP Photo/Haven Daley)

Freeman said her son has lived in Bend all his life. The city, which has a population of about 100,000, lies around 125 miles south-east of Portland.

Police have not yet identified the person who shot the gunman. They said the suspect, whose identity has also not been released, was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported.

‌



At a news conference hours after Thursday's attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised Giamanco, without naming him, for following the gunman into the school. She said he helped end the rampage and likely saved lives as police began arriving at the scene.

"To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," Kotek said.

View 3 Images A police cordon outside Silver Rail Elementary School (Image: AP Photo/Joe Kline)

‌



Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a pupil at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter.

"I think it's miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen told The Associated Press (AP). "I'm feeling very grateful."

The suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said.

Article continues below

It is unclear whether the attacker had any links to the school. He used a pump-action shotgun that had been purchased by his mother, a law enforcement official told AP.

Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if it is provided by a parent or another person with the parent's consent.

The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database maintained by AP and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.

News.title: Student protests spread across Europe as police launch water cannons in clashes across Italy and Albania
News.content:
Gen Z student protests have spread across Europe as scenes of police clashing with young people and shooting water cannons at crowds are seen in several major cities.

Scenes of students taking to the streets started at the end of September in France as young people held protests against underfunding in education. Dramatic scenes from French cities of young people being confronted by riot police as cops make arrests have spread across the continent in countries including Italy, Albania and Belgium.

Thousands of raging students in Italy chanted against the right-wing government as they were hit with water cannons in chaos across several cities.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 8 Images Students burn a cardboard tank in Turin (Image: Camilla Baronetto/JNA via ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Pope Leo urges Vladimir Putin for ceasefire in occupied Ukraine city days after Pontiff's lung cancer op READ MORE :

Young Italians were pictured launching rocks, petrol bombs and firecrackers at police as they protests against school conditions, the cost of living and war. Others were seen spraying fire extinguishers at riot cops while some lit fires in the streets.

In Rome, students marched to the Ministry of Education before throwing smoke bombs and firecrackers at the building. They also chanted against the education minister Giuseppe Valditara, saying: "Valditara, get out of the building."

View 8 Images Thousands of students marching at the Colosseum (Image: Fabio Cimaglia/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Police in Rome warned that they were using video footage to identify those involved in violence, saying: "The actions of this minority group, however, did not impact the effectiveness of the public order management strategy."

In Turin, police used water cannons against protesters and launched tear gas into the famous Piazza Castello, as some young people hurled rocks at cops. Thousands also marched to the Regional School Office where some students flung eggs at police.

View 8 Images Students blocking the streets with bins in Rome, Italy (Image: Marco Di Gianvito/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Similar clashes were seen nationwide, in a day dubbed "No Meloni Day", as demonstrators also rallied against right-wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni. Chaos was seen in Genoa, Venice, Padua and Bari.

‌



Marchers, in a statement, said: "In our schools, every day we see dilapidated buildings, cancelled school assemblies, and a lack of spaces for social interaction and democracy, with all the consequences of the funds invested in the war sector and diverted from schools, universities, and healthcare due to the policies of this warmongering government."

View 8 Images Smoke billows from a fire near a group of protesters in Tirana, on October 14 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Violent scenes have run into their fourth day in Albania as dramatic images showed anti-riot police clashing with protesters in the capital Tirana. Students joined anti-government protesters, who have been demonstrating for months against a luxury tourism project linked to Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner - in a protected area of the coastline.

Dramatic scenes showed youths, seeking education reform, hurling rocks at a police outside the Education Ministry, as riot cops responded with tear gas and water cannons. Though initially peaceful, the rallies turned violent when confronting police cordons.

‌



View 8 Images Student protests have merged with anti-government demonstrations in Albania (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Protesters, on Wednesday, started a fire inside the Education Ministry and attacked several government buildings.

Police have detained several demonstrators. Protesters in masks aimed fireworks at government offices and set fire to trash bins, sending thick clouds of smoke into the air. National police chief Skender Hita, on Thursday, said 71 officers had been injured.

View 8 Images Police officer launches a tear gas canister at protesters in Tirana, on October 16 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday issued a video message from a burned-out college building, saying: "No one can grab Albania by the throat. Anyone who thinks the law does not apply to them is mistaken."

As smaller clashes broke out in at least three other Albanian cities, the country's education minister, Mirela Kumbaro, in a video said: "As minister of education, but also as a mother, I want to share with you a call for cooperation. While the 'dark hands' create dark smoke with destructive actions against public properties and private businesses, we must not let our children near that smoke."

View 8 Images Protesters doused by a water cannon in Brussels, on October 9 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Last week, student protests in Belgium also turned violent as police used tear gas to disperse crowds of young people demonstrating against tuition fees and budget cuts.

‌



They were joined by labour unions demonstrating against budgetary measures from the government. Police made over a dozen arrests as clashes in Brussels escalated.

News.title: Donald Trump fires new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia after five embarrassing days
News.content:
Donald Trump fires new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia after five embarrassing days

Katie Zacharia lasted just five days, one disastrous briefing and mounting questions over her qualifications. Her stint as Trump's mouthpiece lasted half as long as Anthony Scaramucci

View Image Katie made her shaky debut as White House press secretary earlier this week (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump has sacked his new Press Secretary after just five days, one disastrous briefing and mounting questions over her qualifications.

‌



‌



Katie Zacharia was appointed on Monday to replace Karoline Leavitt as Trump's mouthpiece.

‌



But her first briefing for the White House Press Corps on Tuesday invited ridicule, after she took questions for just over five minutes and committed an excruciating gaffe - mistakenly referred to her husband as "my President".

‌



Since then she's been the focus of questions about her qualifications - after having claimed to be a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam.

Announcing her departure as Press Secretary as he left the White House to head to a rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump said Zacharia will stay in the administration in some form, "but maybe in a more pleasant form."

‌



He said he had asked Ms Zacharia moments earlier: "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this. I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led in the last three days."

The rapid departure is reminiscent of the whirlwind career of Anthony Scaramucci, Trump's health of comms for ten days in July 2017. Scaramucci's rapid flameout has become shorthand for the chaos in Trump's first term White House.

Asked on Fox News earlier today if she had the president’s confidence after a rocky start to her job, including scrutiny over claims that she’s a lawyer, Zacharia said: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.”

Article continues below

She also said she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before getting the job.

Zacharia was also asked about the administration’s investigation into Democratic House Representative Ilhan Omar and declined to answer questions, deferring to the Justice Department.

News.title: Angela Rayner: 'Andy Burnham's vow to end rough sleeping is not just a gimmick for Christmas'
News.content:
Angela Rayner: 'Andy Burnham's vow to end rough sleeping is not just a gimmick for Christmas'

EXCLUSIVE: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said she was confident the commitment given by Andy Burnham to offer all rough sleepers an offer of a bed by Christmas would be delivered on

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Andy Burnham's promise to offer all rough sleepers a bed this winter will not just be a gimmick for Christmas, Angela Rayner has insisted.

‌



‌



The Housing Secretary, who is responsible for delivering on the Prime Minister's flagship pledge, said she was confident the commitment would be delivered on.

‌



Ms Rayner told The Mirror's new YouTube show, Sense Check: "The reason I am [confident] is because I have been incredibly proud of seeing the response by the public, by philanthropists, by local government, by mayors, to Andy Burnham's pledge to end rough sleeping.

‌



"That doesn't mean everybody will take that offer, but certainly I've been working with the community and voluntary sector, local authorities, we've put that record investment - £442 million into that."

Pressed on what happens after Christmas, Ms Rayner said: "We continue. We double down. I want people to know that their offer is there. It's not just there for Christmas, it's not a gimmick."

In total there were 4,793 rough sleepers in the autumn 2025 - a 171% hike on 2010 - according to the most recent snapshot data available.

‌



View 2 Images Housing Secretary Anglea Rayner on The Mirror's new Youtube show, Sense Check (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

But the Cabinet minister refused to be drawn on the housing benefit freeze ahead of Chancellor John Healey's maiden Budget on October 28 - but said the policy is "reviewed annually".

Asked how the freeze could be justified, Ms Rayner said: "Local housing allowance has been frozen for a period of time and it's something that is a concern alongside what was section 21 no-fault evictions that were happening at the same time. We've solved that and that and that is something that's reviewed annually.

‌



"But the challenge that we've got is we're putting more money into housing allowance and people are paying more money for rents and on housing than ever before.

"And the problem there is because we don't have the supply. We don't have council housing, we don't have social housing, and we're paying more for less in effect. So therefore we've got to fix that."

View 2 Images Angela Rayner with Chancellor John Healey and PM Andy Burnham on a visit to a homeless shelter (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Ms Rayner - a former care worker - also described being asked to attend one of the new Prime Minister's first major interventions over the summer where he delivered a speech at a care home.

The Cabinet minister said around 20 years earlier she had berated a young Mr Burnham - then the MP for Leigh - as a union rep over issues facing care workers, including short 15-minute home care visits.

Ms Rayner told Sense Check: "Anyway, so then fast forward, and Andy becomes Prime Minister. He puts me back in the cabinet, which I was really grateful for. And then he asked me to attend his announcement he was making over summer at the care home where he was talking about this national care service.

‌



"I'm sat there. And he mentions the 15 minute care calls and he makes his speech without any notes. And I just sat there and I thought, I've waited a long time for a Prime Minister to say that, I was getting emotional.

"Sat there and thinking, this feels different. It feels like he gets it. He'll finish my sentence on things like the ending rough sleeping. He really has an interest in the areas and the things I care about.

"So it's like pushing against an open door, basically. That feels really positive to me. That's different.

Article continues below

"Whereas before, it felt like you had to really fight the arguments, whereas now it just feels like, you're not arguing about what you're doing. You're arguing about how you get there."

News.title: Angela Rayner on THAT vape picture: 'It was put out there to shame, but the public stood by me'
News.content:
Angela Rayner on THAT vape picture: 'It was put out there to shame, but the public stood by me'

EXCLUSIVE: Angela Rayner says image of her vaping on a kayak in Hove last summer - just weeks before her resignation from Keir Starmer's Cabinet - was 'put out there to shame me' but backfired

Angela Rayner hits out at attempts to portray her as a chav

Angela Rayner has hit out at attempts to shame her and portray her as a chav in the right-wing press.

‌



‌



The senior Cabinet minister said an image of her vaping on a kayak in Hove last summer - just weeks before her resignation from Keir Starmer's Cabinet - was "put out there to shame me" but backfired.

‌



Appearing on The Mirror's new Youtube show Sense Check, Ms Rayner said she had been out to celebrate after youngest son's GCSEs at the time. She said: "I had a vape and there was an iconic picture of me.

‌



"It was a dreadful picture - but it was put out there to shame me let's be honest right that's what that picture was about there to say 'look at that chav' and to shame me."

But she added: "The amount of people that contacted me saying I've never felt more represented.

"So that's why I'm saying... when they [the media] go low the public go high. So they've made me a household name because they thought that was clever to attack me at that level.

‌



"The public were upset when they thought I'd done something like broke the rules, they weren't upset because I'm in a kayak. I get that, I don't need the papers to make me understand that.

View 2 Images Angela Rayner says the image of her vaping on a kayak was 'put out there to shame me' - but backfired (Image: Dan Charity / Newsgroup Newspapers Ltd)

"I understand the rhythm of my people who I represent, who I grew up with, I get that they're not interested in. You know, they might have a laugh about it. That's like small fry for them, what they're interested in, what you're doing for us and don't have double standards."

‌



She also dismissed one front page headline - 'Three Pads Rayner' - joking: "Yeah, and I didn't have three pads, either. I have a mortgage. I have a big mortgage, and, you know, probably about 20% deposit, which is my life savings."

She added: "I see online I'm supposed to be a net worth of four million as well. I don't know where that is. I definitely don't have that. But I do recognise now that my circumstances now are very different to the circumstances I grew up in."

View 2 Images Angela Rayner also joked about false claims she is worth £4million (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

‌



But Ms Rayner - who grew up on a council estate in Greater Manchester in poverty before rising through the ranks of the union and Labour movement - said the feeling of not being able to pay a bill never leaves you.

She said: "I can pay my energy bills. I don't have loads of money at the end of the month... but I do live OK. But I know when I was growing up, and when I was at that point as a teenage mum.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

"I know that gut-wrenching feeling when your kid's shoes are knackered and you need to buy a new pair of shoes and you've just got no money. You can't even afford to pay bills. I know how that feels for people and that never leaves you."

The senior Cabinet minister added: "So, I do have this sympathy for people at the moment with the cost of living and what's going on for them, and I know how lucky and fortunate I am compared to a lot of people.

"My poverty was a poverty where my parents were on welfare and I was a free school meals kid. But the poverty that people are facing in Britain today are working people. It is people who have got good jobs, people who are working multiple jobs, and still can't afford to live, because of the costs have gone up and wages haven't gone up to meet those costs."

News.title: New Mirror YouTube show Sense Check hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp
News.content:
New Mirror YouTube show Sense Check hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

The Mirror today launches Sense Check, a hard-hitting flagship YouTube show hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

View 3 Images Actor and presenter and podcast host Nicola Thorp (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

The Mirror today launches Sense Check, a hard-hitting flagship YouTube show hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp.

‌



‌



On the show, Nicola and the Mirror team dive headfirst into the stories dominating the nation’s group chats - from breaking political news to hard-hitting social commentary.

‌



The launch episode features Angela Rayner as Thorp’s first guest. In the episode, Angela insists she didn't consider walking away from frontline politics when she was forced to resign from the heart of government over her tax affairs. She addresses those infamous vaping photos, opens up about the traumatic premature birth of her son and gives an update on the government's commitment to ensuring all rough sleepers have a bed this winter.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Talking to Nicola, Angela said: "I know that gut-wrenching feeling when your kid's shoes are knackered and you need to buy a new pair of shoes and you've just got no money... I know how that feels for people and that never leaves you."

New episodes will be released every week, supported by a rotating panel of guest contributors and Mirror journalists.

‌



The premiere episode is available on Sense Check’s YouTube channel.

View 3 Images The new YouTube show Sense Check is hosted by broadcaster and activist Nicola Thorp

View 3 Images Talking to Nicola, Angela said: "I know that gut-wrenching feeling when your kid's shoes are knackered and you've just got no money" (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Article continues below

Nicola Thorp, Host of Sense Check: "I’m thrilled to be joining forces with The Mirror for Sense Check. With so much misinformation and division online, we wanted to create a show that dives headfirst into the topics everyone is talking about and brings real understanding, great conversation, and a much-needed sense check to the news agenda.”

Chloe Hubbard, Editor-in-Chief, the Mirror: "We need to meet people where they are accessing their news - and today, that’s often on YouTube. Sense Check is our chance to bring our journalism directly to the audiences we know will connect with what The Mirror has to say in 2026, but who may never have picked up the newspaper.

"We’re also delighted to have the brave and formidable Nicola Thorp hosting the podcast. Her fearless, authentic approach makes her the ideal person for this exciting next step.”

News.title: Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
News.content:
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.

These were not the best of circumstances.

Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

In just five days, she was out â the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.

The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered â in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.

"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."

He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".

In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.

News.title: Five days, one briefing: How Katie Zacharia’s short tenure unfolded
News.content:
The White House says Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of the role of press secretary just days after taking the job. It comes after US President Donald Trump said on Friday he suggested to Zacharia she should "reconsider" the job.

Trump went on to say that Zacharia has been treated "very, very badly" by the media in recent days.

The BBC's Sarah Smith, who was in the room at Zachariaâs first briefing, breaks down how her short tenure unfolded.

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
News.content:
UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days.

As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.

The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021.

Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.

It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP.

As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.

The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.

No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.

And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than Â£400,000 from the party.

Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.

Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been.

But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction.

For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal.

We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.

Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that.

"I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said.

"I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."

Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions.

Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.

News.title: Miranda's tears, joy and dance moves steal show as deadly boredom sets in on The Celebrity Traitors
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode six of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

For a show that likes to keep participants and viewers on the edges of their seats, gripped by suspense and skullduggery, it was ironic that Friday's episode of The Celebrity Traitors came down to which one of its stars would die of boredom.

The climactic final scene switched between a series of faces as we waited to see which of the famous faithful would... yawn.

Some dramatic editing and music attempted to build fevered anticipation, but this was a slow-motion, low-energy premise for a murder in plain sight.

The trio of traitors had been tasked with being as boring as possible, and yawned theatrically in one of the castle's communal rooms in the hope that their apparent fatigue would be contagious.

News.title: Faisal Islam: What I learned from a week with the world's top finance leaders
News.content:
When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on.

There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies.

Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity.

At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go.

In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France.

However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions.

In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US.

Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing.

And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Man killed by tiger may have had medical records breached by NHS staff
News.content:
Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.

In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.

News.title: Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show
News.content:
On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.

They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.

The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.

Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.

There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.

Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.

In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, his lawyers said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."

The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.

They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment.

"Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment.

"Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."

The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.

They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.

The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.

Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

News.title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
News.content:
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.

"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

News.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
News.content:
The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
News.content:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.

SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since the Smith Commission report was published in 2014.

The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.

He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".

News.title: Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development.

"Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.

This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.

She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".

In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".

She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.

This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.

She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.

A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project.

"This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess.

"We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing.

"My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."

Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."

The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.

There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".

The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

News.title: Norwegian teen 'hitman' jailed over UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.
