Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about Â£21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

News.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around Â£2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see âthem as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future â prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to Â£3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

News.title: Covid vaccine compensation scheme set for overhaul after Inquiry criticism
News.content:
The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But some people have experienced harm.

In her fourth report, the chair of the Covid Inquiry, Baroness Hallett, called for better support for those affected.

She said while this was a minority, the way they are supported needed urgent reform.

More than 24,000 people have made Covid-related claims to the Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS), a form of financial support paid by the government, but just over 1% have resulted in one-off tax-free awards of Â£120,000.

The report called for "urgent" reform of the scheme, saying that it is "not sufficiently supportive".

It said the current system, in which those affected must show they have been at least "60% disabled", does not work effectively for Covid vaccines.

In its response to the report, the government says, external it is committed to reviewing the scheme to ensure it is "fit for purpose and delivered effectively."

Ministers in England have promised to work closely with the other nations of the UK as well as those injured by the Covid vaccine and their families.

News.title: 3 men sentenced to more than 158 years for the killings of Australian, US surfers in Mexico
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.

The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.

A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.

Antonio Otañez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” But he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.

Here is a look at the key facts and events in the case:

Surfing trip ends in tragedy

The Robinson brothers — Callum and Jake — and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San José, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.

Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.

Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15 meters (50 feet) deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.

The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested García, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.

State authorities said García had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.

García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N,” were also arrested in the case.

Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.

The prosecution’s account and evidence

State prosecutor María Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.

“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she added.

___

Sánchez reported from Mexico City

News.title: Latest vote shows no candidate for UN chief has the required support of all five key powers
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The latest straw poll in the selection of the next U.N. secretary-general on Friday showed that none of the seven candidates has the support of all five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, all of whom have veto power.

This leaves the door open for new candidates if none of the current candidates is able to win over the veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France — in the race to succeed António Guterres, who has led the United Nations for almost 10 years.

As in five previous straw polls, the 15 council members voted to “encourage” or “discourage” the seven candidates or express “no opinion," but this secret poll was the first to use red ballots to distinguish votes from the five powers.

The three leading candidates — U.N. trade chief Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica, U.N. nuclear chief Rafael Grossi of Argentina, and Guyana’s U.N. ambassador, Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett — all received two red “discourage” votes, according to two diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity because the poll was private.

Grynspan, a former Costa Rican vice president, remained at the top of the polling with nine “encourage” votes.

While it was not known how each council member voted, numerous U.S. officials have made clear for the past several weeks that none of the candidates is ideal from the perspective of the Trump administration. It has focused on radical reform of the global body and the withdrawal, or planned withdrawal, of the United States from multiple U.N. agencies.

However, despite the administration’s differences with the U.N., its bureaucracy, and reservations about who the next secretary-general should be, the officials have not ruled out supporting one of the announced candidates.

The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said the U.S. position was still being refined and would be made clear in the coming days.

U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz told reporters as he left the closed council meeting that the U.N. needs “strong, energetic leadership” that is going to take the 193-member world body back to its original focus on peace and security.

“This institution, after 80 years, has tried to become everything to everyone,” Waltz said. “We put it on a diet so to speak — we’re all a little better off after being on a diet — and (need to) get it focused on peace and security.”

By tradition, the job of secretary-general rotates by region, and this is Latin America’s turn. There also is pressure to pick a woman, who would become the first female leader of the U.N.

“We understand there is a desire for regional rotation,” Waltz said. “Of course, if the best candidate is a woman, we would welcome that — but we really just need the best candidate.”

The two candidates at the bottom of Friday's straw poll were women — Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a former General Assembly president and foreign minister of Ecuador, and Ivonne A-Baki, a former Ecuadorian ambassador. Two African contenders — former U.N. diplomat Olara Otunnu of Uganda and Senegal’s former president, Macky Sall — each received 10 “discourage” votes.

The next straw poll, with red ballots, will be held next week, the two diplomats said.

Waltz and Russia’s U.N. Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia both left open the possibility of new candidates.

“We're going to get this done, I'm confident, before the end of the year,” Waltz said. “That is my wish, definitely,” Nebenzia said.

___

AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed to this report from Washington

News.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's attorneys demand return of property seized in federal search of her home
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar asked the Justice Department on Friday to immediately return property that federal agents seized from her home this week, arguing that the search stemming from an immigration fraud investigation was “neither justified nor lawful.”

In a letter obtained by The Associated Press, lawyers for the Democrat from Minnesota described the investigation as a baseless effort to go after a longtime political target of Republican President Donald Trump, noting that the search was conducted just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.

Omar's attorneys wrote that there is "no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status."

“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers," Omar's legal team wrote in the letter first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

A Justice Department spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment Friday evening.

Monday's search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home this week drew swift condemnation from Democrats, as the Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.

Federal authorities seized Omar's phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the probe told the AP this week.

The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork. Separately, Washington's U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and her office is probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.

In the letter, Omar's attorneys accused the Justice Department of violating longstanding agency policy designed to avoid potentially influencing an election. They also raised concerns about whether the department appropriately followed all of the specific instructions by the magistrate judge who approved the search.

In addition to the return of her property, Omar's attorneys are demanding that the Justice Department preserve any audio and video that was taken during the search, according to the letter.

Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.

According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” She became a lawfully naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.

Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”

The search of her home came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ.”

News.title: A humble oyster pail turned takeout icon: The American story of the Chinese food carton
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It's an icon, that small white receptacle made from a single piece of cardboard folded into a trapezoid-shaped box. Sometimes there's a wire handle, sometimes a bright red graphic of a Chinese-style pagoda on the side. And inside, deliciousness.

The Chinese takeout container — at least, as it's commonly seen in the United States — is actually about as American as it gets, with its mix of ingenuity, immigrant cultures becoming homegrown staples, and the desire for convenience (also known as sitting at home in your PJs.)

The idea of what is essentially a paper bucket dates to 1894, when inventor Frederick Weeks Wilcox was granted a patent for what he called “a new and useful improvement” for pails used to carry oysters. A single piece of material would be folded in such a way that it would have structural stability while also limiting the ways it could leak, and also incorporate a lid.

That's the container. What about the contents we assume are inside it?

Chinese immigrants started coming to the U.S. in the mid-1800s, taking part in the Gold Rush and working to help build the railroads. The communities they created, known as Chinatowns, rose up in places like San Francisco and later around the country. They included eating spots where the foundations of an Americanized style of Chinese food was laid.

After World War II, there was a “real profusion of Chinese restaurants, diversifying away from just chop suey and chow mein ... we see this explosion of interest and growth in Chinese food,” says Michelle King, professor of Chinese history at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Crucially, it was also the start of an association in the public mind of Chinese food with cheaper prices, availability and convenience, she said. And restaurant owners wanted to be considered accessible, for which takeout played a part, she said. “You need to take it home, you have a dinner party you want to cater for, we can do that for you, right?” King says.

At some point in the 1970s, at a packaging company then known as Fold-Pak, the pagoda design was added, sometimes along with words printed in a font used to stereotypically evoke an association with Chinese culture.

“It kind of becomes claimed as a Chinese American food eatery item, like the pizza box or something like that might be for Italian food,” King said.

These days, takeout cartons come in a variety of shapes, and the food landscape has expanded to include a range of cuisines that might show up in the former oyster pail.

Even so, it IS still an icon — quite literally. Check your emojis for “takeout.”

___

Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

News.title: Selma Blair's representatives say she didn't intend to hurt anyone on flight that led to her arrest
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Actor Selma Blair did not intend to harm anyone during a flight and its aftermath where she is alleged to have assaulted two flight attendants, a police officer and a nurse, according to a statement Friday from her representatives.

The long statement sought to push back against what it said were inaccurate and unsympathetic portrayals of Blair, 54, and the Delta flight from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday that led to her first arrest.

“Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight,” the statement said. “There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”

A previous statement along with her lawyer's remarks in court had said briefly that a medical emergency was behind all that happened, but the new statement gave a more detailed defense.

Blair has multiple sclerosis, and without specifying she had done so, the statement said it is “outrageous” that anyone would suggest she doesn't.

“Her diagnosis has been public since 2018,” the statement said. “What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle. She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily. Selma also has pseudobulbar affect, a neurological condition secondary to her MS, which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her.”

The statement added: “For the same reason, she travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side, and the authorities took her dog from her.”

The statement said she has been a relentless advocate for disability rights and the MS community.

Blair was accused of injuring two flight attendants on the plane bound for John F. Kennedy Airport, then kicking a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she got there, according to a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.

She pleaded not guilty Monday to two counts of assault on state charges involving the officer and the nurse, and a judge issued a protective order for them. She is free on bail, and her next court date is in January.

The FBI also issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

Authorities have released few details of what happened aboard the plane.

In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asked the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but said ambulances were not necessary.

The Michigan-born Blair began acting in New York in her early 20s. Her major film roles have included 1999’s “Cruel Intentions,” 2001’s “Legally Blonde” and 2004’s “Hellboy.”

In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she later regretted during a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles. She said she had mixed alcohol with medication, causing her to black out.

Friday's statement said the public version of the more recent events has “been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline.”

“A handful of journalists have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline, and we are grateful to them,” the statement said. “But fair reporting has been the exception, and in the space left by our silence, speculation has hardened into something being treated as fact.”

___

Dalton reported from Los Angeles.

News.title: Painting Eisenhower Building would diminish historic character of White House complex, report says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump's plan to paint a 19th-century historic landmark building next to the White House would diminish the historic character of the White House complex, the Trump administration concluded in a draft environmental assessment published Friday.

Trump has suggested the massive Eisenhower Executive Office Building be painted as part of his push to remake and beautify the nation’s capital. The plan, estimated to cost at least $7.5 million, has alarmed preservationists, architects, historians and others who argue that granite is not meant to be painted and that paint would trap moisture and degrade the stone.

Trump last year said the building's gray exterior is a “really bad color.”

The building's architect, Alfred B. Mullet, hand-selected the construction materials, which “are central to the building’s historic character and original design intent,” the environmental assessment concluded.

The EEOB and the Treasury building, a similarly massive and unpainted stone building on the other side of the White House, form a “visual hierarchy” at the seat of government, which has been in place for 125 years and would be disrupted by a paint job, the report said.

“The White House is by comparison much smaller in size and scale, but its placement at the center of the grounds and white color communicates its importance,” the report said.

The proposed white mineral silica paint is permeable enough that it would be unlikely to trap moisture and damage the stone, the report found. Preliminary tests suggested the paint could eventually be removed with minimal damage to the stone, but more testing is necessary, it said.

An alternative proposal to clean and restore the building while improving the exterior lighting would not affect its historic character, the report found.

News.title: RAF jets report ‘unidentified drones over UK’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Royal Air Force has had close encounters with two unidentified drones in British skies this year, it has been reported.

Jets flagged two “near miss” incidents that took place days apart during simulated air combat training and an air-to-air refuelling exercise over the North Sea, according to The Telegraph.

One was reported near Norfolk and the other near Humberside, and both were spotted at altitudes above 10,000ft. These sightings were reported to the police and “multiple different external investigations” are ongoing, according to logs seen by the publication.

It is not clear whether the drones were hostile or not at this stage, The Independent understands.

open image in gallery A Royal Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon FGR4 conducts a display for spectators during Scarborough Armed Forces Day ( Getty )

Drones typically must fly below the legal height of 120 metres (400 ft) to reduce the likelihood of coming across other aircraft, according to the UK Civil Aviation Authority.

Sightings at such a high altitude are uncommon, but not unprecedented, as military and civilian pilots have reported suspected drones at similar altitudes which have been considered by the UK Airprox Board.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson did not comment on the incidents directly, but said they were remaining vigilant in how they assessed potential drone activity.

“Our enhanced vigilance and improved detection capabilities have increased our ability to identify, record and assess potential drone activity and we’re investing more than £2 billion into wider air defence and counter-drone capabilities, including the upgrade and sustainment of the Typhoon fleet,” they said.

“We remain highly vigilant to the potential threats posed to defence and stand ready to respond appropriately through our measures and capabilities that keep our Armed Forces safe.

“While reports of drone sightings are not necessarily hostile, where activity is assessed to pose a credible threat, Defence has measures available to respond appropriately and we do not comment on specific threat assessments.”

open image in gallery The Ministry of Defence said it remains vigilant to potential threats posed to defence ( PA Wire )

The report comes a month after The Independent exclusively reported that rogue drones were targeting Britain’s military bases almost daily.

Some 340 security incidents involving drones were reported at or near MoD sites in the year to August 2026. In 2025, there were a total of 250 incidents recorded – double the 126 recorded the year before.

Experts have warned that the alarming increase suggested the government was not prepared to combat hostile threats amid growing escalation from Russia and aggression from Iran.

Former Tory defence minister and former Army captain Tobias Ellwood told The Independent the large sharp uptick in detected drone incidents in the UK showed that the government was “asleep” to threats to the British military, which had become a “target”.

He said Russia and Iran were “100 per cent” responsible for many of those incidents. “They are absolutely active in Britain in plotting, mapping, and then recruiting useful idiots to prosecute this targeting.

“It could be criminal gangs as well, but they would then be supported by Russia. Russia is by far the obvious culprit here... It’s not China’s style. They tend to do things in a different way.”

The Armed Forces Bill is set to become law by the end of the year, which will give personnel the power to take out drones posing a threat to defence sites across the air, land or water without assistance from the police.

News.title: More than half of Brits asked by businesses to make payments in cash, new data reveals
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

More than half of consumers (54 per cent) said in September that they had visited an business in the previous eight weeks that encouraged cash payments, according to research commissioned by cash access and ATM network Link.

Such encouragement ranged from notices indicating that a business accepts or prefers cash, to staff directly asking patrons if they could pay in physical currency.

The findings revealed that venues requesting cash included cafes and restaurants, independent shops, hairdressers, barbers, beauty salons, outdoor markets, pubs, retail stores and supermarkets.

Graham Mott, director of strategy, Link, said: “These results show cash remains a practical choice for millions and that many small businesses are actively encouraging its use, making a resilient ATM network more important than ever.

open image in gallery Among those who were asked to pay with cash, three-quarters of people said they did complete their purchase using coins or banknotes ( PA )

“It’s also fascinating to see when prompted, most people are happy to pay with cash and still choose it for certain retailers and services.”

Among those who were asked to pay with cash, three-quarters (75%) of people said they did complete their purchase using coins or banknotes.

People in Northern Ireland were particularly likely to say they had been encouraged to pay in cash, at 69% – and were also particularly likely to have completed their purchase in cash – with 88% of those asked doing so.

People in Scotland and Wales were also particularly likely to have obliged by paying cash, with 82% and 78% respectively doing so.

YouGov surveyed more than 2,100 people across the UK between September 10 and 11 for the research.

It follows a report that one in seven high street businesses have gone cashless in the past year.

The biggest driver to becoming a “cashless” business in the survey was fraud prevention, followed by security concerns and a lack of customer demand.

News.title: Asia’s vaccine self-sufficiency drive gets $650m boost
News.content:
An “innovative” partnership to boost vaccine security across Southeast Asia will inject up to $650 million into regional manufacturing, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported shots.

The five-year initiative, announced at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok on Friday, will see major lenders, non-profits, and the private sector come together to invest in the region’s vaccine industry.

Currently Southeast Asia’s production base remains limited and exposed. The majority of shots are imported, and any capacity the region does have is highly concentrated – one analysis this year estimates 60 to 90 per cent sits with a single vaccine manufacturer.

Even before Covid-19 hit, this vulnerability was recognised. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), a regional bloc of 11 countries, endorsed a vaccine security and self-reliance initiative in 2019, driven by Thailand’s National Vaccine Institute (NVI).

These concerns have mounted since the pandemic, but up until now investment as well as political will has been lacking. The partnership announced on Friday, led by NVI, hopes to remedy this, and develop a model that can be copied worldwide.

​​“If we can do it here in Asia, then that really provides a model for the world,” said Aurélia Nguyen, deputy CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a a vaccine research non-profit. “We can build it out in Africa, in Latin America, and that really gives us the resilience that we want the next time we have a major epidemic.”

Cepi has committed up to $20 million of “catalytic funding” for the programme, which is backed by the World Bank as well as organisations like the Singapore-based AVPN investment network.

In all, the package of loans and grants will include at least $174m in public financing, and up to $460m in private capital mobilisation for regional vaccine manufacturing. Further details, including recipients, have not yet been announced.

But Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, told a panel in the Thai capital that “we believe this has the ability over time to mobilise up to $650m of finance”.

He added that the group would use public loans and grants alongside investments by its private-sector arm, the IFC, while its guarantee arm, MIGA, would help cover investors against risk.

“It’s really important because each element of the World Bank Group is involved in it,” Donohoe said. “We’re not just talking the talk, but walking the walk.”

Speaking to the Telegraph after the event, Nguyen added: “Innovative models and partnerships like this, where we’re each bringing a piece to de-risk scientific technology, [allow us] to leverage larger quantities of capital.

“But I think what’s also helpful in this model is, beyond the financing, [we] have a sort of coordinating umbrella through Asean,” she said. “So you can be smart and [avoid] duplicating investments, which brings commercial sustainability and resilience for health systems.”

Nakorn Premsri, the director of NVI, added that the investment model will help “build a more sustainable and resilient regional vaccine ecosystem, to meet both routine needs and the demands of health emergencies”.

News.title: Are my smart home devices always watching me? How to stay safe (and private) in a connected house
News.content:
The past decade has seen a huge rise in the number of smart devices in the home, from video doorbells to robot vacuum cleaners.

Smart connectivity offers many useful upsides, from letting us keep an eye on package deliveries to streamlining household chores. However, concerns remain about whether these devices are safe from hackers and how they might impinge on our privacy.

As a technology journalist for almost 20 years, I have reviewed many smart appliances and have lots of connected devices in my own home, so I’m an experienced user. To find out more about their potential downsides, and how to keep yourself protected, I’ve also spoken to an expert from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, a board member at the Connected Standards Alliance (CSA) – which promotes openness and safety within smart-device networks – as well as other leading brands in the space.

What is a smart appliance?

A smart appliance connects to your home network, often via Wi-Fi, to allow for a wider range of interactions. That might be a washing machine that notifies you when it’s finished, or a fridge-freezer such as the Samsung Family Hub with a screen and voice controls.

But smart appliances don’t have to be huge: connected lightbulbs, baby monitors, smart plugs and more can all link up with your home network, in many cases integrating with voice assistants such as Amazon’s Alexa or Apple’s Siri.

News.title: Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Economy slows before Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
The Chancellor said banks are too often seen as “distant financial institutions”, in a sign he will not raise taxes on the industry in the Budget.

John Healey has faced pressure to impose a windfall tax on bank profits to help rebuild an expected decline in his wiggle room in the public finances.

John Healey said: “My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.

“That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the Budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

“And my special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future. That the resilience that the IMF has reported on this week by upgrading our growth figures in the UK this week, that the welcome monthly growth figures published this morning reinforce, and importantly, alongside that, the IMF reports said that Britain stands out for our deficit reduction plans, and will have his forecast actually a reflection not just on forecast plans but performance over the last couple of years. You know, a consolidation plan in place and underway.

“I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me, I will meet those fiscal rules in full.

“That will be part of the Budget that I set out in two weeks’ time, and I think the IMF report reinforces that that is not just a not just a reinforcing the strength of Britain’s position, but something that they say they want to see other countries doing as well.”

News.title: Ukrainian Vampire drones drop food on town besieged by Russian army
News.content:
On Ukraine’s front lines, drones are the deadliest weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal, hunting Russian soldiers one by one with chilling precision.

But across the Dnipro River, the same machines have been given a very different mission: keeping trapped civilians from dying of starvation.

Since March, Ukrainian drones have been flying food and medicine into occupied Oleshky, on the river’s left bank, where residents are surviving on grass and weeds.

The town is less than three miles from Kherson, a city battered by Russian drones and shelling.

Since December, Oleshky has been under an effective blockade. Its roads are mined and shops have closed, with no food arriving by road since late May. Humanitarian agencies are blocked from entering, and the health system has all but collapsed.

Only around 2,000 of its 24,000 pre-war residents remain. For them, the drones are now their only lifeline.

“With the onset of winter, the situation is only getting worse,” said Elvina Osmanova of the Kherson regional military administration. “Food supplies are running out. People are facing a life-threatening choice: risk their lives trying to find food outside the city or remain without food.”

News.title: Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle
News.content:
When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Sports.title: Regulators are right that football has massive problem with money – but clubs are much more than simply businesses
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL has a financial problem. It may also be about to acquire a regulatory one.

The Independent Football Regulator’s ‘State of the Game’ report this week delivered a grim verdict on a £9billion industry.



Ninety-four per cent of clubs are losing money. Aggregate losses have reached £1.7billion.

More than a quarter of clubs could not survive a month if their owners stopped paying the bills.



The figures are alarming. But football has never been a business for the faint-hearted.

And the question is whether the regulator intends to make it safer, or simply less ambitious.

There was precious little financial security before the Premier League was born in 1992.

In the early 1980s, attendances collapsed, clubs struggled to pay the bills and some sold their grounds to local authorities to survive. A 1982 report found the 92 league clubs were collectively losing £6m a year.

Football did not emerge from that crisis by discovering the joys of financial caution. It reinvented itself. The Premier League broke away, secured its own broadcasting deals and built a commercial phenomenon. Average Prem club revenues have since grown more than 30-fold.

That is the inconvenient truth for anyone who believes football can be regulated into prosperity.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Its success was built by people prepared to take risks, invest money and imagine their club could be something greater than it was.

I sat through every Prem meeting on these issues and every House of Lords debate on the legislation.

And I understand why football needs proper safeguards. I also know how easily a well-intentioned intervention can have consequences its authors never anticipated.

This is why I have repeatedly warned in the House of Lords against treating football like a bank.

Financial resilience matters, but a football club is not simply a business seeking to minimise risk.



It exists to win promotion, avoid relegation and, occasionally, achieve something extraordinary.

If regulation makes every decision about survival rather than success, a football club that avoids risk may be condemned to mediocrity. Financial sustainability matters, but so does sporting jeopardy.

Promotion, relegation, ambition and the possibility of an unlikely triumph are not unfortunate side effects of football’s business model. They are the business model.



Nobody wants another Bury, another club disappearing while its supporters are left wondering how it happened.

Owners who spend money they do not have can do lasting damage to communities.

But a regulator that tries to eliminate every financial risk could eliminate much of the reason people invest in football in the first place.

There is a difference between stopping reckless spending and stopping clubs from spending. It is a difference the regulator will need to understand.

Take cash. The IFR is right to worry about clubs that cannot survive a month without fresh money from their owners. Bills do not accept promises and players cannot be paid in potential.



But cash is not the same as value. Football clubs own or control valuable assets: Players, stadiums, training grounds and commercial rights.

The IFR does consider squad values in its solvency analysis.

Yet the distinction between a club with a temporary cash-flow problem and one with an unsustainable business matters.

The recent valuation of Behdad Eghbali’s Chelsea at a massive £5bn shows the extraordinary capital value that football can generate. Assets are not cash and valuations can evaporate in the blink of an eye. But neither should financial health be reduced to a snapshot of the bank balance.

The real problem is that clubs are caught in a vicious circle.



Financial rewards for reaching the Prem are so vast, that Championship owners are tempted to spend beyond their means to get there.

Telling clubs to behave more cautiously does not remove that incentive. It tells them to compete with one hand tied behind their backs.

Meanwhile, the money is not always going where it should. The IFR says agents’ fees reached £484million in 2025-26.

Nearly half a billion pounds went to intermediaries, while clubs across the pyramid struggled to balance their books.

There is surely more scope to tackle waste here than in the ambition to build a better team.



Nor can the growing gap between the Prem and the EFL be ignored.

The top flight is the financial engine of English football, it funds the entire pyramid as it is.

More money flowing down the pyramid may be part of the answer. It cannot be the whole answer if it simply fuels higher wages, transfer fees and agent commission.

The regulator must also understand what it should not regulate.

Consider Manchester City. IFR chair David Kogan said decisions about whether owners are fit to run a club must be based on evidence and statutory tests, not diplomatic relationships.



He has pledged to resign if political interference compromises the regulator’s work. That independence is essential.

The Newcastle takeover provides a warning. In 2021, then-Prem chairman Gary Hoffman told clubs the Government had applied pressure over the approval of the Saudi-backed deal, while insisting that the pressure had not influenced the decision.

Hoffman announced his departure weeks later amid a backlash over the handling of the takeover.

Kogan must be free to assess City’s owners on the evidence, just as he must be free to reach a conclusion that ministers may dislike.

A regulator that can be swayed by political convenience is not independent.



One that uses its independence to expand its own reach without restraint is not necessarily wise.

In the House of Lords, I set out three tests for the regulator: Protect growth, remain light-touch and exercise independent judgement.

Those are not just concessions to football’s richest clubs. They are safeguards for the entire game.

The IFR’s report is a warning and it deserves to be taken seriously. But a warning is not a licence to treat every club as a problem to be managed, and every owner as a risk to be contained.

English football has never been free of financial danger.



Its success has come from taking risks, attracting investment and turning a domestic competition into a global business.

Now the challenge is to make that success more resilient, not regulate away the ambition that created it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The sun is shining on a £9bn industry. The regulator is right to ask what happens when it rains.

But it must not mistake carrying an umbrella for building a better football club.

Sports.title: Leeds hero Paul Robinson says James Trafford has the swag to be the next Elland Road Premier League goalie great
Sports.content:
Next

GOALKEEPING legend Paul Robinson knows what it takes to be Leeds United and England No1.

Now he says James Trafford can cement his own name into Elland Road and Three Lions folklore as he prepares to shut out Manchester United.



Trafford has fast become a hit with supporters following his £45m club-record arrival from Manchester City this summer.

The 24-year-old hit his first bump in the road in last week’s defeat at champions Arsenal, his first setback since Daniel Farke made him the undisputed first-choice.



But Whites hero Robinson says the star has the swag to brush off that setback when hated rivals the Red Devils head to LS11 on Sunday.

And, given time, he has all the attributes to emulate the glory days of himself and fellow great Nigel Martyn between the sticks for Leeds and England.



Robinson, speaking exclusively to The Sun via Hellotickets.com, said: “The key to any legacy or if you’re part of a list of players when you look back at a club, it’s longevity and it’s doing it over a long period of time. Being No1 and performing at a consistent level.

“We’re very early on in his Leeds’ career and very early on at the start of the season, but if the start is anything to go by, if he can continue that level of performance for a number of years, then he’ll be talked about in the same conversations, absolutely.

“It’s very important that he stays at that level and that Leeds stay in the Premier League, which they’re looking like they’re going to do very comfortably this season. They’ve had a brilliant start to the season.”

Robinson, who came through Leeds’ academy to make 119 appearances before joining Tottenham in 2004 after relegation, continued: “You can see his body language and the way that he’s relishing the number one.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“There’s two different types of goalkeepers. Some like to have a really good number two and always be on edge, knowing that they’re not necessarily guaranteed to play every week. Some enjoy that whole stigma and the confidence and the whole thing about being number one around the training ground, being number one around the dressing room.

“It seems to be a position that James Trafford is really relishing in.”

Farke led Leeds to survival last term following promotion and the FA Cup semi-final.

With the club’s ambitious owners already working on expanding Elland Road, the squad was strengthened with £34.1m Bosnian defender Tarik Muharemovic, free transfer Harry Wilson and Trafford during the summer.



The bright start to the campaign has got fans dreaming again. And a victory over bitter rivals United will only make them even more confident of a push for Europe.

Robinson, who deputised several times for the injured Martyn in Leeds’ memorable run to the Champions League semi-finals in 2001, said: “It just feels a really good time to be a part of the football club and that the club’s in a really good place.

“It’s moving forward in every single aspect, the development off the field, the development and progression with the team. But you’ve got to ward against expectation, because it’s the old adage, with success comes expectation.

“Leeds had to stay in the Premier League last year, they did that, and now this season people said, ‘Leeds look like an established Premier League team’, or ‘Leeds could push for Europe’, but at the start of the season they were saying they would be in the conversation about going down again.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They have got the building blocks to be pushing for European places again. The expectation will come because the team’s playing so well and that’s only natural, but the foundations that this era, that this generation is built on, there’s every chance that they could go on and push for European places.



“They’re certainly looking at the top half of the table and not below them, that is for sure. They are looking at a very strong, established Premier League side who have the foundation to go on.”

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca reveals his KIDS are backing Man City fans’ bizarre banana craze before firing warning to haters
Sports.content:
Next

ENZO MARESCA’S kids are rallying for inflatable bananas — and the Italian hopes the craze gives Manchester City an extra potassium boost.

And the Etihad boss trusts fans won’t peel back on their “us against them” mentality when the “sham” club returns to Prem action on Saturday.



Maresca insists the sea of yellow was not just a one-time thing for the club’s first away match at Liverpool since the guilty verdict broke.

The 46-year-old has now appealed to match-goers to save an inflatable banana for each of his four sons at City’s first Premier League home game since the club were found guilty of over 100 charges.



The Italian said: “Very nice! I hope to see many bananas in the stadium. I didn’t know the history behind the banana.

“It creates a nice environment for the fans and for everyone that is in the stadium.

“I have four kids. They already asked me, but they’re going to be at the stadium and we’ll see.”

City, who deny any wrongdoing and are appealing the verdict, were found guilty of using “sham” contracts to artificially inflate revenue by £830m between 2009-2018.

The away end waved bananas during City’s 3-0 win at Anfield’s bearpit as a bright visual symbol of loyalty against the noisy backlash.

Blow-up bananas became popular among City fans in the 1980s and 1990s when they spent time in the second and third tiers, and have been revived in reaction to the threat of being punished with relegation.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

SunSport understands City have ordered nearly 11,000 inflatable bananas from cult-hero Imre Varadi’s balloon business.

Ex-City striker ‘Imre Banana’ has also been invited as a VIP guest today. It’s understood City CEO Ferran Soriano initially wanted 60,000 balloons for the 3pm blackout.

Quite a haul, considering the Etihad holds 61,000.

Ipswich’s away section won’t match Anfield’s ferocious hostility, but City can expect far more ‘cheat’ jibes than they faced in their 4-2 midweek loss to Paris Saint-Germain.

While the banana craze brought welcome light relief to the Maresca household, the Italian has avoided slipping up before the press since the verdict was delivered.



The former Chelsea manager cautioned the rest of the Prem that the ongoing controversy has provided added motivation for his players.

He said: “Ruben Dias said people don’t like City winning, so that is why we like to win. That is a good message for everyone.

“Since the noise I can see the fans, the club, the team more together. There is noise around the club but we need to try to make our noise.

“That means winning at Anfield and trying to beat Ipswich. This is the way we can make our noise. We are not able to control the other noise.”

City added one of the UK’s top lawyers Mark Howard KC to their defence team in their fight against the verdict.



Maresca, who took charge during the summer, revealed that he has not spoken to anybody outside of the club to get a different perspective on the scandal.

He said: “I am a ‘respect’ person so no because I completely trust the club. So I don’t need people from outside the club to understand the situation more.

“The club have explained the situation to me clearly and I trust the club 100 per cent, I trust the people that run the club and this is the reason why I took the job.



“I don’t feel any kind of stress about the outside situation because it’s something I don’t control. I just focus on how we can try to win on the pitch.”

Maresca revealed ex-boss Pep Guardiola did not feel the need to address the dressing room after the rollercoaster PSG affair on Wednesday night, with the Catalan legend returning in a show of support to the board.

He added: “It was great for the fans to see Pep at the stadium. This will always be his house.

“I saw him after the game, I didn’t see him before. We were only talking about the match, the first half, the second half.”

An expected victory over Ipswich will give Maresca the best start of any top flight manager since the Prem launched in 1992, beating Guardiola’s record of six straight wins at the start of his reign a decade ago.



With Phil Foden returning from his three-match suspension following his derby red, Maresca hinted at resting several stars.

Erling Haaland, who scored a double against PSG, Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez and Marc Guehi were name-checked as potential rotators.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ipswich, who splashed £189.5m in the summer to outspend Manchester United and Barcelona, sit 10th in the Prem.

The new boys are coming off a huge win over Fulham and all three of their victories have come via 90th-minute goals, presenting a potential banana-skin for City.

Sports.title: ‘It’s intolerable’ – Real Madrid call for LaLiga chief to quit after ‘extraordinarily serious’ Nazi claim
Sports.content:
Next

REAL MADRID called for LaLiga chief Javier Tebas to quit after he accused the club of techniques used by Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.

Tebas has claimed Real’s communication and in-house TV channel “recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels”.



He later clarified he was drawing comparison with “those propaganda techniques” and “not with an ideology”.

But Real responded: “The repeated conduct of Javier Tebas shows a lack of neutrality, respect and impartiality incompatible with his responsibilities.



“It is intolerable and extraordinarily serious that he should resort to a comparison with the propaganda methods of the Nazi regime to discredit our club, its management and its television.

“His attacks on Real, and those who demand transparency, constitute a real scourge for Spanish football.”



Real are yet to shine following Jose Mourinho‘s return to the Spanish capital as they sit fourth in LaLiga after eight matches.

The club are six points behind undefeated league leaders Barcelona, with an “icy atmosphere” developing in the dressing room under the Special One.

Matters have been made worse with star striker Kylian Mbappe suffering an ankle injury on international duty with France.

Vinicius Junior is also facing a spell on the sidelines after receiving a four-game ban for a hair pull in Real’s win against Villarreal.



However, there has been some good news with Jude Bellingham agreeing a monster new five-year deal with the Spanish giants.

Real host fifth-placed Sevilla in LaLiga on Sunday.

Sports.title: Glam Man Utd Wags forced to cancel night out after being put ‘on lockdown’ following Martinez’s team rant
Sports.content:
Next

THE partners of Manchester United stars have been forced to cancel a night out in the wake of Lisandro Martinez’s criticism of club bosses.

The glamorous group were set to enjoy a night out at an Italian ­restaurant on Thursday evening.



But they have been put “on lockdown” to limit the fallout after Argentinian defender Martinez hit out at player recruitment earlier this week.

It meant their scheduled evening at Cibo in Hale, Gtr Manchester, had to be put on the back burner.



A source said: “The girls were looking forward to getting together for a nice meal out and a whole floor of the ­restaurant had been booked.

“But they had to cancel it at the last minute after the club closed ranks in the wake of Martinez’s comments.



“Everyone was told to just keep a low profile in the hope it all blows over.

“The Wags are very protective of their partners and some are less than impressed with what he said because it sounded like he was saying some of his teammates aren’t good enough.”



Some of the players had also been due to have a night out at Cibo, a favourite of former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson, but cancelled their reservation too.

Martinez’s glamorous partner and former carnival queen, Muri Lopez, was due to attend, along with Harry Maguire’s wife Fern Hawkins, plus Ana Pinho, who is married to captain Bruno Fernandes.

Others said to have booked a spot included Marcus Rashford’s girlfriend Lucia Loi as well as Luke Shaw’s long-term partner Anouska Santos.



The source added: “Some of the girls naturally gravitate towards each other because they are from South America or European countries like Portugal while the English girls also have a close bond.

“Generally as a group they all get on very well and try and meet up a few times a year.

“But this week it was decided being pictured out on the town when the club is in crisis wouldn’t be a good look, for players or their partners.”



Martinez accused the club’s director of football of not doing enough to improve the squad after United’s 2-0 Champions League defeat against Atletico Madrid on Tuesday.

He apologised two days later, and is part of the squad to face Leeds United in the Premier League tomorrow.

Sports.title: I loved Lisandro Martinez’s honesty but hated his apology – Man Utd ace s*** the bed and looks like a muppet
Sports.content:
Next

I LOVED the honesty of Lisandro Martinez’s comments this week — but hated the apology.

And I have lost a load of respect for him because if you are going to stand there and say what you think, then own it.



If you truly mean it, then b******s. You are not getting me to apologise.

In my opinion — and I’m not privy to the Manchester United way of doing things — he has been told two things can happen.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

They are likely to have said: ‘You’re going to take the fine and apologise — or you are not involved at the weekend.’

And he s*** the bed. So what he said on Tuesday is irrelevant now. If you are going to draw that line in the sand, then draw it really deep.



This all just makes him look like a muppet.

I thought he was an overrated player anyway. They talk about him being this bull because he competes. But isn’t that what we are supposed to do?

And my six-year-old competes, I don’t call him a bull. I say, ‘Well done, but you’ve got to be better to be a professional’.

What this has shown is, you can say you care so much about the team and getting better — but it actually just shows you care more about your money.



You are going to get fined and you want to play because you are out of contract at the end of this season.

At that level, two weeks wages is a drop in the ocean. So it’s not just the money side of it, Martinez knows he is not going to play.

I know United have got the one-year extension option but, essentially, he is out of contract.

If they wanted to keep him, they would have just extended his deal at the start of this season.

Clearly, he had a chat with the agent, who said: ‘Look, there are not that many feelers out there, so you have to play really well this year.



‘Then hope United have a good year and you have some good games in the Champions League.’

That’s ultimately why he is p****d off. In the Champions League, on the biggest of nights, he’s playing next to Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven.

Yoro played for France in the last international break, so it can’t really be about him.

Clearly, he is looking at Heaven and thinking, ‘You are not good enough to be here’. But Danny Murphy said something the other day and he was spot on. And I was annoyed that I didn’t say it!

What player ever wants more help in their position? No one. It’s like me going, I wish we had another striker.



Well, if you bring a striker in for X amount, the club is under pressure to play that person.

I get Martinez saying we need a bigger squad. But what he is ultimately saying is, we need to think about every position — except mine.

Martinez has been there nearly five years. He has won a World Cup in that time.



I agree that the standards might be low at United right now but if you’ve won a World Cup and you’ve also played with Lionel Messi, you know what the best looks like.

So, you should be the one setting the standards. But Martinez seems to be the guy that goes with the pack. If the pack is good, he’s good. If the pack is s***, he’s s***.

And people should know dressing rooms are like classrooms. Let’s say there are 30 people.

You’ve got five people who don’t want to be there — they are the bad kids.

You’ve got five who are amazing. They want to be there and love it.

And then you’ve got 20 in the middle and they sway depending on how the mood goes.



Last season, those 20 swayed so there were 25 at the good end. Now, very quickly, that 25 has gone down to about 15.

They are saying, ‘This is rubbish, it’s the owners’ fault, the board’s fault, the manager shouldn’t be here’.

It’s a low-hanging fruit because the fans will like them for this. Martinez is saying what the fans want to hear.

But, make no mistake, Elland Road is the worst place for Martinez and Co to go right now.

If I am a Leeds player at this moment, I am thinking about how we can run riot on Sunday. I could not have picked a better game.



Everyone is talking about the Atletico Madrid defeat and they are forgetting the Tottenham match. They got spanked by Spurs.

United have won two games all season — but they were against Ipswich and Sabah.

I don’t really know what they are as a team, but they run less than anyone else in the league. I’d love to be in Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s shoes.

I would be saying to the lads, ‘First ten minutes, just keep putting it in behind Martinez and let me chase him.

‘Let me kick him, push him, maybe stand on his fingers when he falls on the floor. Let’s see if I can get him to bite as he’s already hot-headed.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

‘Let’s see how nervous he is and what he is really made of.’

Martinez needs to have an exceptional game.

Sports.title: United States GP: UK schedule as F1 returns to COTA
Sports.content:
Following an extended stint across Asia, Formula 1 heads to America for the United States Grand Prix at the iconic Circuit of The Americas in Austin, Texas.

After the previous triple-header saw Kimi Antonelli move closer to a maiden F1 title, the Mercedes driver enters three more back-to-back races knowing he has every chance of sealing a historic triumph.

The Italian is 102 points clear of his Mercedes team-mate George Russell at the top of the standings, with the first two victories of the year for Red Bull and Max Verstappen only having helped Antonelli move clear of the pack, leaving him with a small chance of being crowned champion in Austin.

While both Antonelli and Mercedes are in remarkably strong positions in the championships, the competitive picture has rarely been more exciting during the 2026 season, with each of the top four teams entering each weekend with genuine hopes of victory.

Many eyes will be on Antonelli, but Verstappen's quest to complete a hat-trick of wins, along with Lewis Hamilton's attempts to bounce back from a tough Sunday in Singapore promise to provide plenty of entertainment.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the F1 Show podcast, Bernie Collins considers whether Lewis Hamilton has lost trust in Ferrari after overriding a team strategy call in Singapore.

United States GP track - Circuit of the Americas

Of the newer permanent circuits to have joined the calendar over the past couple of decades, the Circuit of the Americas is certainly one of the very best.

The undulating 3.4-mile, 20-corner layout built on the outskirts of Austin quickly proved a hit with drivers when it made its debut in 2021 as F1's first made-to-measure home in the USA.

There was also a sense of familiarity given its track design took inspiration from some of Europe's most famous tracks.

An Esses section reminiscent of Silverstone's legendary high-speed Maggotts and Becketts complex at Silverstone makes up Turns Three to Six, while a reverse triple-apex challenge in the style of Istanbul Park's Turn Eight and a Hockenheim-style arena section all feature in the exciting anti-clockwise lap.

The circuit even has its own signature feature in the form of a steep uphill run to the first corner, which has been the scene of numerous overtakes and controversial incidents over the past 13 years when drivers go wheel-to-wheel into the wide braking zone before powering back downhill towards the Esses.

United States GP weather in Austin

Temperatures are expected to climb above 30 degrees Celsius on all three days of track action, but the wild card is whether rain is going to play apart.

The latest forecast suggests there's a 50 per cent chance of rain falling during the race, with showers also possible on Friday and Saturday.
