World.title: Cop killed, others injured in Sligoville gun battle
World.content:
ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — An ongoing gun battle in Sligoville, St Catherine, has left several cops injured and at least one lawman killed, according to reports reaching Observer Online.

The Observer understands that the incident began about 5:15 am on Friday when a team from the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations unit was conducting an operation in the Five Miles area of Sligoville in search of wanted men.

The cops were reportedly clearing a building on a premises when they came under gunfire from two men who had barricaded themselves inside the house among other occupants.

During the exchange, a young girl who was inside the building reportedly sustained gunshot injuries. It is understood that she managed to escape from the house and was taken to hospital by a police team.

Sources described her condition as serious but stable.

Members of the JCF’s SWAT Team, Area 5 Area Fugitive Apprehension Team (AFAT), the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) and other police personnel are on the scene as the operation continues.

More information to come.

— Llewellyn Wynter

World.title: DOMESTIC DISPUTE TURNS FATAL
World.content:
Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey who reportedly committed suicide after stabbing his wife who was taken hospital where she is said to be battling for life.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — The usually quiet community of New Market Oval in Savanna- la-Mar has been left in shock following a violent family dispute that left a nurse battling for life in hospital and her husband dead.

The husband, Nesta Anderson, a window maker and disc jockey, was from a neighbouring community. Police report that the couple had been involved in a dispute at their home when the woman was allegedly stabbed by Anderson.

Following the attack, Anderson used a ratchet knife to inflict stab wounds to his abdomen about 10:30 am Thursday.

He was rushed to hospital where he was pronounced dead. The Jamaica Observer was told that the couple, who had been together for more than a decade, has three young children.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the children witnessed the incident. When the Observer visited the community, police were processing the scene, while residents shied away from speaking publicly about the matter.

President of the Cooke Street Benevolent Society Bishop O’Neil Russell said he spoke with Anderson just a few days ago and that the incident came as a complete shock as the family was known to be quiet.

“We had a conversation because, you know, there were some things that the benevolent society was supposed to do for him.

We are always in constant dialogue, but he had not shown any sign of depression. It is so shocking. It comes as a shock to see really what took place,” stated Russell.

Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division), who visited the scene, expressed sadness over the tragedy.

“It’s not anything to rejoice over. We all have issues, and we all have problems. We all go through things,” stated Chang.

She noted that the community, which was devastated by Hurricane Melissa last October, is already under stress and attempting to rebuild.

“We understand the constraints, but you know, we have to deal with our problems better than this, instead of taking our own lives or taking the lives of others,” stated Chang, who joined Russell in calling on people having problems to seek help.

Domestic violence, it can affect anyone regardless of our income, education, or social status. It stretches across all socio-economic backgrounds. We just have to understand that it is right in our midst and we should not be ashamed of it.

We should seek help. And I implore the persons in the Savanna-la-Mar Division, or anywhere for that matter in Jamaica, to seek help because I’m sure there are telltale signs even before it occurs,” Chang said.

She also emphasised the need for community sensitisation to stop judging victims and instead offer support, “because we all deserve to be safe in our own homes”.

World.title: EU leaders clash over migration, Ukraine and budget in Brussels — but delay big decisions
World.content:
Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU.

Luc Frieden and Emmanuel Macron speak ahead of a round table during the EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels.

But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.”

“In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded.

World.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
World.content:
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.

Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.

Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.

"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.

He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
World.content:
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

World.title: Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
World.content:
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.

That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”

The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.

While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.

SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.

The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
World.content:
The stark warning comes as Kyiv heads into a brutal winter and faces a cash crunch.

BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia.

“Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.”

In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat.

Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.

The Ukrainian president traveled to Brussels to meet with European leaders and shore up financial support for his embattled country. While the EU is Ukraine’s staunchest backer, the bloc’s list of priorities is stacked with rising energy costs, looming elections, geopolitical crises and an impasse over its €2 trillion budget.

World.title: Denmark, Italy, Poland urge EU leaders to harden stance on irregular migration
World.content:
The bloc’s 27 leaders were due to discuss migration during a special session on Thursday requested by Meloni and Frederiksen following a tense back-and-forth with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in June.

Tensions have risen further after Spain’s Ceuta exclave was overwhelmed by migrants during the summer and as far-right parties have made gains around the bloc.

The draft also “calls the Commission to explore [a] possible consultation mechanism to encourage coordination on national measures potentially affecting other Member States while respecting national competencies.”

While the last phrase does not name any one country, Sánchez has clashed with Meloni over his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis as well as Spanish measures to regularize around 1 million migrants.

However, language discussing the impact of migration on social housing was removed from the draft over concerns that it could be perceived as provocative toward Spain.

One of the diplomats — who, like the others, was granted anonymity to discuss confidential information — said the updated draft was unlikely to win unanimous support from all the leaders, but had been proposed to bring the language closer in line with political sentiment and spark debate.

World.title: Spanish opposition leader Feijóo calls for navy to be deployed to Ceuta
World.content:
Feijóo’s calls for a “firm response” are the latest in a wave of criticism of Sánchez’s government after more than 70,000 migrants arrived in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the Moroccan border in late July. Migration ministers across the European Union have in recent months repeatedly demanded tough new EU migration policies.

His comments also come after unconfirmed reports that a Moroccan patrol boat remained in Spanish waters off the coast of Ceuta for hours Thursday, which the Spanish Civil Guard has denied. Moroccan warships also allegedly entered Spanish waters in July, though a European Commission spokesperson told Spanish press agency EFE Wednesday that it was “up to the Spanish and Moroccan authorities to clarify the facts.”

Feijóo spent Thursday morning at a summit of the center-right European People’s Party — of which the PP is a member — in Brussels, during which the EPP lashed out at the Spanish government over the Ceuta crisis in its closing statement, according to POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook. Conservatives have said they will implement measures to curb immigration if the government swings to the right after the snap election.

“Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again,” Feijóo said in an opinion piece earlier this month.

Tensions over Ceuta and Melilla — which Morocco considers occupied territories — are becoming increasingly strained: A POLITICO poll earlier this week revealed that 58% of respondents believe an armed conflict between Madrid and Rabat is “likely” within the next decade.

In a landmark visit to the exclaves also this week, King Felipe VI said that Ceuta and Melilla were “an inalienable part of the political and national reality that is Spain. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country are not negotiable.”

The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories was in 2007, when former King Juan Carlos I traveled to Ceuta and Melilla amid a diplomatic spat with Morocco.

World.title: Sanchez rejects criticism of Spain's migration policy: 'Words do not match reality'
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday rejected criticism from several European leaders over Spain's migration policy and defended his government's approach to tackling irregular immigration and managing migration flows.

 

"If you look at the facts, at the figures - which is kind of always what happens with the far right - it's like night and day," he said in Brussels, where he is attending the European Council summit. "What is being said has nothing to do with reality (...) one thing is the blah, blah, blah and another is reality."

Sanchez was responding to comments by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, who have questioned the Spanish government's migration policies, particularly its extraordinary regularisation plan for migrants.

Sanchez drew a distinction between his disagreements with the Danish prime minister and the Czech leader's criticism, which he likened to far-right rhetoric.

"With the Danish prime minister we have disagreements, but indeed, it has nothing to do with what the prime minister of the Czech Republic said, which, by the way, sounds very much like what the far-right Vox says in Spain," he said.

Babis had accused some European leaders of being willing to "replace the population" to stay in power and warned that his country could tighten border controls to prevent migrants from arriving from other EU countries.

Stocker, meanwhile, described Spain's regularisation plan as a "bad signal", arguing that it could have consequences for the EU as a whole. Frederiksen has called on the European Commission to examine the implications of Spain's measures.

Sanchez points to Spain's record

In response to the criticism, Sanchez argued that Spain is making progress in controlling irregular arrivals and cooperating with countries of origin and transit.

"The migration and asylum pact that we secured under the Spanish presidency is working," he said, adding that Spain is "a model pupil" in the fight against irregular immigration.

The prime minister cited interceptions in the Atlantic, returns and refusals of entry at airports as examples of Spain's migration policy. He also rejected claims that Spain is part of routes used for secondary movements of migrants within the European Union.

"The reality, the data show that Spain is pursuing a very responsible policy in the fight against irregular migration, in managing regular migration flows and in cooperation with transit and origin countries," he said.

Sanchez also stressed the importance of maintaining a progressive government in Spain, arguing that "because Europe indeed needs a contrast of opinions and political positions", and urged his European partners to continue implementing the migration and asylum pact.

Von der Leyen calls for stronger external borders

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the need to move forward with implementing the EU migration and asylum pact and strengthening cooperation between member states. She noted that irregular crossings of the EU's borders have fallen by more than 56% over the past two years.

Von der Leyen outlined three priorities for EU migration policy: fully implementing the migration and asylum pact, strengthening the management and protection of external borders, and improving preparedness for potential border crises.

She also announced that the Commission will propose strengthening Frontex, the EU's border agency, to expand its capacity to support member states when needed. She stressed that responsibility and solidarity must go hand in hand, while acknowledging that more work remains to be done.

"To succeed, it is necessary to continue acting together," von der Leyen said, as European leaders remained divided over how to manage migration and tackle irregular arrivals.

Some countries push for changes to summit conclusions

Denmark, Poland and Italy pushed for changes to the summit conclusions, including an indirect reference to Spain's plan to regularise the status of 600,000 undocumented migrants. Spain and France opposed the proposed changes.

A revised draft seen by Euronews urged member states to avoid "measures that may create incentives for illegal migration". However, the broader wording was ultimately rejected in favour of a shorter, less forceful version.

The draft also called on the European Commission to strengthen coordination between national migration policies that could affect other member states. The proposal, jointly backed by the three countries, was seen as an implicit criticism of Spain's left-wing government.

Macron backs Spain

French President Emmanuel Macron said after the summit that "ideological divisions" between EU member states over migration were making them "ineffective", while expressing support for Spain over the Ceuta crisis.

"We have had a bad debate," Macron said. "My assessment is that when we politicise this debate at the table, we create divisions. And when we are divided and fall back on national solutions, we become ineffective," he added.

Macron described the Ceuta crisis as a "humanitarian tragedy" and noted that France had not signed the letter sent to Brussels by 22 EU countries.

"Spain was the target of a hybrid attack," he said, adding: "There was no need to wait until today to know who attacked Spain just after what happened in Ceuta."

World.title: Pope Leo XIV urges Putin to agree to truce in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, calling for a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine while recovering in hospital from lung cancer surgery.

 

The Vatican said that Pope Leo "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population".

Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said it was "the Holy Father who took the initiative" to call Russian President Vladimir Putin "to plead the case of this besieged city, where around 2,000 civilians need safe routes out and humanitarian corridors."

"I believe the Pope asked for a truce to allow both the delivery of humanitarian aid, especially food, and the evacuation of those who must leave the city."

"I hope," added Parolin, "that when faced with a request from the Holy Father, President Putin will agree to implement what has been asked of him."

According to a statement reported by Russian news agencies, President Vladimir Putin thanked Pope Leo XIV for his willingness to help resolve the conflict in Ukraine and for his humanitarian initiatives. He also wished the Pope a speedy recovery following his recent surgery.

Previous contacts between Moscow and the Vatican

This is the second time Pope Leo XIV and Russian President Vladimir Putin have spoken.

The two leaders previously held a telephone conversation on 4 June 2025, less than a month after Leo XIV's election.

Pope Francis last spoke with Putin on 17 December 2021, his birthday. Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, however, his attempts to establish direct contact with the Russian president were unsuccessful.

World.title: Trump's new press secretary leaves after less than a week following controversy
World.content:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her role just days after taking office, following criticism of her press briefing performance and questions over her resume.

 

Asked about reports that Zacharia was "transitioning" out of the role, a White House official confirmed the news to AFP news agency on condition of anonymity.

Several US media outlets, including The New York Times, reported that Zacharia had been fired. However, US President Donald Trump denied dismissing her, saying she had been "brutalized by the media", as reported by Fox News.

He told reporters he had encouraged her to reconsider the role just minutes earlier, telling her, "You don't have to do this if you don't want to."

US President Donald Trump boards Marine One as Katie Zacharia and White House aide Natalie Harp look on in Alaska, 13 October 2026. AP Photo

Zacharia's first White House press briefing on Tuesday lasted less than 15 minutes. She began by listing what she described as Trump's achievements before taking just three questions from reporters.

Appointed less than a week ago, she faced scrutiny over her legal credentials after failing to give a clear answer about where she had passed the bar exam, which is generally required to practise law in the United States.

Although Zacharia holds a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged on Thursday that she had not passed the bar exam, a requirement to practise law in the United States.

In an interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, Zacharia confirmed that she had never retaken the exam.

"It was never my intent to go into the practice of law," she said.

Speaking to pro-Trump outlet Real America's Voice on Thursday, Zacharia said she had registered for the exam but became "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.

She also claimed that "many people in the field" had told her she could "label myself a lawyer" because she held a law degree.

World.title: Romanian president calls for greater NATO oversight in the Black Sea in Euronews interview
World.content:
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.

 

“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.

The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.

“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”

He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.

“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.

The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.

The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.

However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.

Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.

“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.

The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.

Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.

“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.

Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.

However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.

Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.

Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.

“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.

Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.

He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.

“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.

“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”

Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

World.title: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.

 

The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.

Here are the five highlights.

Rallying behind Ukraine

The bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.

Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.

The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.

“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”

“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.

In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.

The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.

Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.

EU budget

On Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.

One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.

European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.

Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.

That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.

Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.

Migration

Migration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.

This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.

Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.

But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.

“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.

Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.

Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”

By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."

China

On “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.

Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.

China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.

While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.

The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.

The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.

“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.

Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.

Energy

On Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).

The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.

The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.

“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”

Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

World.title: Albanian PM blames 'foreign hands' for escalating anti-government unrest
World.content:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama called for calm on Friday, blaming unnamed "foreign hands" for the unrest as protesters demanded his resignation for a fourth consecutive day.

 

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace," he said in a Facebook video.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand, the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once."

Thousands of young protesters took to the streets of Albania’s capital, also demanding education reforms, with some smashing windows and damaging traffic lights.

"The government's indifference and arrogance since the beginning of our movement have been unbearable and have made the situation worse," said the high school student, who asked to be identified only by her first name.

Protesters set rubbish bins on fire to block roads and threw stones at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannon.

"We are not criminals. We simply want a better life for our parents and ourselves. We do not want to leave Albania," 18-year-old Ledia told AFP.

Riot police fire tear gas at protesters during an anti-government demonstration in Tirana, Albania, Friday, 16 Oct., 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The demonstrations, which began on Tuesday, have since spread beyond Tirana to other Albanian cities, with students boycotting classes amid growing anti-government unrest.

This week's escalation comes after months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, including demonstrations against a luxury tourism project linked to Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has become a symbol of alleged corruption and inequality in Albania.

On Wednesday, the European Union delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities, expressing concern over “the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana.”

Rama's Socialist Party won a fourth consecutive election victory last year, with the next parliamentary elections not scheduled until 2029. His government is aiming for Albania to join the European Union by 2028.

World.title: Global timekeeping rules change: leap second scrapped from 2027
World.content:
The world’s official time standard will stop adding leap seconds from 20 May 2027. The General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) decided to end the practice on Thursday 15 October 2026.

 

The resolution was adopted at the conference’s 28th meeting in Versailles, where delegates discussed the future of world time.

Until now, leap seconds have been added from time to time to keep atomic time in line with the Earth’s rotation. But from 20 May 2027, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) will run continuously, with no interruptions.

Why the leap second is being scrapped

The old rules were meant to keep two different ways of measuring time in step. UTC is based on extremely precise atomic clocks. Astronomical time depends on the Earth’s rotation, and that rotation speed varies slightly.

To keep the gap between the two time scales small, 27 leap seconds have been added since 1972. The most recent was at the end of 2016. As a result, one minute could exceptionally last 61 seconds.

These corrections are barely noticeable for people, but they can cause technical problems. Computer systems, telecoms networks, satellite navigation and power infrastructure all depend on precise, reliable time synchronisation. Past leap seconds have already disrupted computer systems and online services.

Earth’s rotation makes new rules necessary

One reason for the decision is the way the Earth’s rotation is evolving. A negative leap second raised new risks.

Over very long periods, tidal forces slow the planet down, but in recent years it has at times been spinning slightly faster.

That raised the possibility that, for the first time, a so-called negative leap second might be needed, with a second removed rather than added. Because this has never been done, it is uncertain how reliably technical systems would cope.

The international expert community therefore chose to end the existing rules ahead of schedule. Under the new regime, the gap between UTC and astronomical time will be allowed to grow, potentially reaching 3,600 seconds, or one hour.

Experts believe, however, that it will still be some time before such a gap would actually require any correction, so the measure is essentially precautionary.

The CGPM: little known, but many member states

The CGPM brings together representatives of member states and of associated states and economic areas and usually meets every four years.

According to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), it currently has 69 member states and 34 associated states and economies.

In Europe, they include Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Poland and Ukraine.

The Americas are represented by the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico and Peru, Asia by China, Japan, India, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, and Africa by South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Kenya. Australia and New Zealand are also represented.

What does this mean for the UK?

For everyday life in the United Kingdom, the decision will not bring any immediate change.

Scrapping the leap second is a technical adjustment to the international time reference and must not be confused with the familiar switch between summer time and winter time.

According to the GOV.UK Clock Change Guide, the clocks go back one hour on Sunday, 25, October, 2026, at 2:00 AM.

The statue of Winston Churchill stands in Parliament Square, backdropped by the Elizabeth Tower, commonly known as Big Ben, in London, Wednesday, June 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Alber AP Photo

As such, the local clock time in the UK will still follow Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), which is UTC+0 in winter, and British Summer Time (BST), which is UTC+1 in summer. Seasonal time changes will be unaffected.

A step towards more stable world time

The impact will be felt more strongly in specialist fields that need exceptionally precise alignment with the Earth’s rotation. These include astronomy, geodesy (the science of measuring and mapping the Earth and determining its shape, size and gravitational field) and certain satellite-based applications.

For these disciplines, accurate knowledge of the Earth’s rotation will remain crucial. Because leap seconds will no longer tie world time to that rotation, they will have to account separately for the growing gap between clock time and astronomical time when necessary.

In principle, the aim of the new rules is to make international timekeeping simpler and more reliable in the long term. In particular, digital systems will no longer have to cope with extra seconds being inserted at irregular intervals.

World.title: Commission and Ukraine launch joint task force over EU accession
World.content:
The European Commission announced on Friday a joint task force with Ukraine to speed up accession work, after Hungary lifted its veto on opening further negotiating clusters.

 

EU and Ukrainian officials will sit on the task force, which is meant to help Kyiv complete its accession homework. Earlier this week, member states agreed to open two more clusters. The remaining two are now expected by the end of the year.

“Ukraine is among the countries making most progress towards EU membership. Following the opening of two more negotiating clusters this week, I discussed the next steps with PM Serhii Koretskyi. We agreed to launch a joint Task Force,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said on X.

The task force will focus on the so-called interim benchmarks, the mid-process targets a candidate must meet before it can start closing negotiating chapters.

It will work through a list of outstanding requirements under the benchmarks on the fundamentals of accession, namely the rule of law and anti-corruption reforms.

“This is an important step to have a joint task force that will be meeting in fact twice a week over the next several months to really try to accelerate the work,” Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews.

Hungary’s veto was lifted only after Kyiv agreed on an education law for the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. The Ukrainian parliament passed the law with a broad majority, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy swiftly signed it.

The vote raises hopes that Ukraine’s political elite will keep up the broad consensus needed to adopt the reforms required for EU membership.

"The task force follows the model used for Montenegro and Moldova," a Commission official told Euronews, adding that it gives Ukraine’s accession process new momentum.

Kyiv is also due to receive a roadmap breaking up the main steps, and an indicative timeline to complete the accession process as part of a broader enlargement package expected at the beginning of November.

“This step shows our commitment to supporting Ukraine’s path to EU membership. Our success will require unity and commitment from all involved Ukrainian partners,” Kos said.

Sasha Vakulina contributed to the reporting.

World.title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions on hold
World.content:
The US president cited national interests for his decision to sign a waiver on sanctions Congress voted to place on Russia.

US sanctions on Russia will not take effect as planned after President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving them for national security reasons.

"As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act," the executive order said.

"I have submitted to the Congress ​a certification that ‌the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the ​United States," ⁠Trump said in the order released by the White House.

The White House did not immediately explain how Trump's decision to pause the sanctions will serve the national interest.

The decision was notified on the White House website late in the evening. It noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

Trump's controversial deal with Russia

The Lindsey Graham Act, which was named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill had found bipartisan support in the Congress and was passed in September.

It allowed the Trump administration to increase pressure on Russia over its war against Ukraine by imposing duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil.

The move to waive the sanctions against Russia comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try and bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

​India, one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, was among the countries that raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.

World.title: Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
World.content:
The latest figures show that 3,335 square kilometers of the Amazon rainforest were cleared in the year ending in July, the lowest level since 1988. The drop has been described as an "historic achievement."

Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.

According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.

The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.

The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.

It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.

The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'

"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.

"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.

"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.

"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.

Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.

The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.

World.title: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump
World.content:
EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.

Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.

Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.

Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.

Is the US siding with Russia?

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.

President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.

When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."

How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."

He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.

The Starlink slowdown

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine's budget problem

Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.

"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."

The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.

Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.

Ukraine to 'keep living and fighting with dignity'

Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.

The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: West Bank: US journalist injured by Israeli settlers
World.content:
Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine said she was beaten by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Reporters Without Borders slammed the attack as "brazen violence."

Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday after being attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while on assignment in the occupied West Bank, according to the publication.

The Post said that the incident took place near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, and involved "dozens of masked Israeli settlers" who attacked Palestinian villagers gathering the autumn olive harvest.

Washington Post says Levine clearly identifiable

Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.

"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said. Levine is a US citizen.

"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."

Speaking from a hospital bed later, veteran photojournalist Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me."

Blogger Andrey Khrzhanovskiy filmed the incident and told The Post that the settlers beat Levine with sticks while journalists and villagers were forced back.

West Bank olive harvest under attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Netanyahu's office says facts 'remain unclear'

The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement saying it was not yet clear exactly what had happened.

"The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.

Netanyahu's office went on to say there were reports that "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths." It said that there was footage of masked individuals from both sides "hurling objects."

"Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," Netanyahu's office said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that both the IDF and the Israel Border Police attended the scene.

"Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist was injured during the confrontation. All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said in a statement on X.

"The IDF strongly condemns this incident. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the IDF said.

Palestinian American watches as West Bank house under siege To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US condemns 'criminal violence'

The US said it condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the AFP news agency quoted a State Department official as saying, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers.

"The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the official told AFP.

US Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Connecticut, in a post on X, called the attack "appalling" and said "there must be swift justice and accountability for perpetrators of violent extremism in the West Bank, which stands in the way of regional peace and is escalating an already unpredictable and dangerous situation."

EU to impose new sanctions against Israeli settlers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Attack condemned by press association and advocacy group

The Foreign Press Association represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories and said Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment were stolen by the attackers.

"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.

"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added.

International press watchdog Reporters Without Borders strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault."

"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.

World.title: White House press secretary Zacharia exiting role after short tenure
World.content:
Zacharia, having served only five days in the role, is now the shortest-serving press secretary in White House history. Her departure follows a rocky debut at the podium and controversy surrounding her background.

New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is on the way out from her position, The New York Times and other US news outlets reported on Friday.

Zacharia's departure leaves Trump without a key spokesperson with a little over two weeks before November's midterm elections.

Zacharia's week on the job

Zacharia started her new role just five days ago, taking over for Karoline Leavitt. She had a nervy first White House briefing with journalists on Tuesday, fielding just three questions and leaving the podium after fewer than 14 minutes.

The White House website said later that day that "Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary."

Earlier on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested that Zacharia might be leaving. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be ​happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump ​told reporters.

He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If ​I ‌were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"

Controversy over Zacharia's legal background

Last Friday, Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as the new press secretary. However, she became embroiled in controversy when it was revealed that her earlier claims of being a lawyer were false.

Until last week, Zacharia was a commentator for conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax. She also advised Trump Media and Technology, the company behind Trump's Truth Social platform.

Zacharia has also long described herself as a lawyer, but her credentials remain unverified. While she graduated from law school, neither she nor the White House has provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She was also a general counsel at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell, from 2024 to 2025. Grenell served as acting director of national intelligence in 2020.

Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. While nearly all licensed US lawyers first obtain a law degree, law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.

World.title: Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?
World.content:
Girls wearing headscarves have been turned away from schools in Azerbaijan, triggering unusual protests involving children. The government rules do not mention hijabs. Why are schools enforcing unwritten rules?

A dispute over Islamic headscarves in Azerbaijani schools has triggered protests at home and an unusual exchange of criticism between politicians in Azerbaijan and Turkey, two countries whose leaders routinely describe their relationship as that of "one nation, two states". The row has raised questions about religious freedom, sovereignty and the limits of Turkish and Iranian influence in the south Caucasian country.

The unprecedented protests have been taking place across Azerbaijan for a nearly week. Children have demonstrated against the headscarf ban introduced at schools. Among those rallying outside of schools are girls who wear Islamic headscarves; others, including boys, have joined classmates in solidarity.

Rallies in general are rare in a country where police routinely disperse any public protests. But demonstrations involving children are unprecedented in Azerbaijan. As the videos showing the protests started spreading on social media, access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted in the country, indicating how seriously the authorities are taking the issue. Internet monitors documented blocks; the authorities have not explained their cause.

School rules interpreted as a hijab ban

The dispute follows a series of legal changes. On July 7, Azerbaijan amended its general education law, reinforcing the principle of secular education and requiring pupils and teachers to comply with dress codes. On September 21, the government adopted Resolution No. 309, tightening school uniform rules.

The resolution prohibits additional clothing that disrupts the standard uniform or conflicts with secular education. It does not explicitly mention the hijab ― a Muslim headscarf covering the hair and neck ― or instruct schools to exclude pupils wearing one. But some school administrators have interpreted the rule as applying to hijabs and turned girls covering their heads away. The regulation gives each school's pedagogical council responsibility for resolving compliance issues.

A separate decision on October 6 set dress requirements for teachers. Reports followed of women wearing headscarves being prevented from teaching.

The new rules from the government in Baku don't explicitly mention the hijab Image: Chen Junfeng/Xinhua/picture alliance

Secular education and religious freedom

Azerbaijan is a predominantly Muslim country, but Article 18 of its constitution separates religion from the state and requires state education to be secular. Articles 42 and 48 protect the right to education and freedom of conscience.

Supporters of the schools' actions say the same dress rules should apply to all pupils. Critics argue that excluding girls because of religious clothing violates their rights. The dispute cuts across conventional political divisions: some government critics support the restrictions, while some non-religious Azerbaijanis oppose them. School headscarf restrictions also prompted protests in 2010 and subsequent years.

Families and teachers describe the impact

A Baku literature teacher with 40 years of experience, said that girls wearing headscarves were not admitted to classes at the teacher's school. Some removed their scarves; others went home or wanted to study at home. The teacher, who didn't want to be identified by name and provided only the initials M.C., supported enforcing the uniform rules, arguing that children were too young to make decisions about religious dress.

A parent identified as D.A. told DW this was not a nationwide hijab ban, but a matter of school uniforms. Another parent who opposed the restrictions withdrew an interview before publication.

Facebook user Sarraf Cabbarov from Baku posted on his social media account that his daughter Sevil, a primary school teacher in Azerbaijan's capital, was dismissed for refusing to remove her headscarf. He also published a school order issuing her a written warning under the new dress regulations.

Detentions and reactions in Azerbaijan

On October 12, the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained in connection with the protests. According to the ministry's statement, the group had confronted school staff, damaged property and attempted to obstruct school activities and traffic. A criminal case was opened under Article 233, concerning disruption of public order. The ministry did not identify those detained or say whether they included children.

Hijabs are part of daily life in Baku Image: Osman Karimov/AFP

Artist and activist Ilkin Huseynov went missing after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with pupils affected by the restrictions. Local media later reported, citing people close to him, that he had been given 30 days of administrative detention for allegedly disobeying police orders.

Some observers linked the introduction of the new rules for school uniform to the attempts by the Azerbaijani government to counter the influence of neighboring Iran and the growing strength of religious groups within the country. This interpretation is, in essence, echoed by government officials as well, although they stop short of explicitly naming Iran.

Fazil Mustafa, who chairs the Committee for Public Associations and Religious Institutions at Azerbaijan's parliament, said the authorities were concerned about religious groups influenced from abroad and defended the school rules. Allahshukur Pashazade, head of the Caucasus Muslims Office, also warned of outside interference but called for a peaceful solution. The alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established.

Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls wearing hijabs and called for the release of anyone detained solely for protesting peacefully.

Dispute reaches Turkey

The controversy has also drawn criticism in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul on October 3. Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticized the restrictions, saying it's unacceptable to deny education to students wearing headscarves. Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party replied that close relations did not justify interference in its internal affairs.

For affected families, the immediate question remains whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

Sinem Demir contributed reporting.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: At summit, EU leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
World.content:
President Zelenskyy has received words of encouragement from EU leaders, who pledged support for Ukraine's self-defense against Russia. This comes as winter approaches and the US seems to be withdrawing support.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?

"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."

"One ​thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will ​not lift any sanctions unless Russia ⁠stops ​this ​war."

The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.

After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."

Diesel deal between Trump, Putin angers Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine

Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that ​they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."

"The winter package is not only energy, ​it's also air defense and funding," he added.

During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.

"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.

When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.

Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.

"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."

Trump denies responsibility for restrictions on Starshield

Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.

However, on Friday, Trump denied that he or Starlink founder Elon Musk were responsible for these restrictions. "I don't think it was me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump told journalists.

He added that any limit to Ukraine's access to the Starshield system was not imposed by the United States.

Musk had said that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company, SpaceX, which operates Starlink.

Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Europe is working to help Ukraine with satellite and early warning systems.

"We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed," Macron told reporters.



Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM

The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.

"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."

Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.

After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.

"I ​assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his ​country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.

The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.
