Ensenada, Mexico: The three Mexican men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad have each been sentenced to 158 years in prison. A court in Ensenada announced the sentence on Friday (Mexico time), one week after the three men – Jesús Gerardo (also known as “El Kekas”), Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús – were found guilty. Debra Robinson outside court after three Mexican men were convicted of killing her sons Callum and Jake. AFP The men’s full names were not identified by the court for legal reasons. A translated statement from the attorney-general’s office said the men were each sentenced to 158 years and nine months in prison; 135 years for aggravated homicide; 10 years and 9 months for aggravated robbery involving violence; and 13 years for the violent theft of a vehicle.



The Robinson brothers’ parents attended every day of the trial and were present last week when the men were found guilty. Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson. Nine News Debra and Martin Robinson held hands as judge Raúl Hernández Arellano read out his verdict as it was translated by an aide. There was no jury. “Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad,” Martin Robinson said outside the court. “While no verdict can ever bring back our boys, or ease the heartbreak of losing them, we hope this outcome represents an important step towards justice and accountability.



“Callum and Jake had their whole lives ahead of them, filled with dreams, love and promise. We will forever carry their memory in our hearts … They will never be forgotten.” The Robinsons speak to the media after the verdict. AFP The Robinson brothers and Rhoad disappeared in late April 2024 while they were camping in a remote surfing spot in beachside Baja California. Their bodies, along with that of a local farmer, were found days later at the bottom of a well. They had been shot. The prosecution successfully argued that the three tourists were victims of a robbery that went awry. The court heard the victims begged for mercy before they were murdered, and that the killers later mocked their pleas. Gerardo’s then-girlfriend, Ari Gisell, is already serving a 20-year sentence for instigating the robbery that led to the murders. She gave evidence that Gerardo had confessed to the crime. “I f---ed up three gringos,” he told her.



Jake, 31, was a doctor who was due to start a job at a hospital in Geelong when he returned to Australia. Callum, 32, was a talented sportsman who had played lacrosse professionally in the US. He was living in San Diego. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold Will Weissert and Meg Kinnard October 17, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. November’s midterm elections will hinge in large part on Americans’ attitudes toward the cost of living, and the polls show the public giving the president poor marks for his handling of the economy. Bloomberg Trump personally signed the legislation just last month. Named after late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, it had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine. Trump’s unexpected move comes a week after he stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia. A poll by the AP-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research published on October 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress on Election Day on November 3.



Graham died in July but had advocated for stricter US sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine. His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation – then changed his mind on Friday. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress. Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.



The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death – with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy. The president’s latest action also followed him announcing last week that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president as he condemned Volodymyr Zelenskyy for striking Russia’s diesel refineries. AP Photo/Nathan Howard Trump said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Trump’s decision to strike a deal with Putin on diesel on the world market has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike, who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine – without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.



The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centrepiece for Senator Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister, who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. Related Article Analysis

Trump diplomacy Trump promised to end the Russia-Ukraine war in a day. Now he’s funding it In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions A single bid secures keys to inner west home for $150,000 below reserve Robyn Willis October 17, 2026 — 1:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A woman from Greenacre bought a home in Croydon Park for $150,000 less than the reserve with a single bid on Saturday, paying $1.3 million at auction. The woman was the only registered bidder for 16 Brighton Avenue and initially made an offer before the auction starting of $1.25 million for the well-presented two-bedroom semi, which was guided at $1.35 million. However, Rich & Oliva sales agent Marco Errichiello convinced her to raise the offer with a formal bid of $1.3 million and the property sold. “She said that was the maximum she could afford to spend with the current rate rises,” Errichiello said. “[The vendor] thought it was better to have a sale in these conditions rather than wait.”



The two-bedroom semi has retained many of its original features. Domain The vendor has held it as an investment. Records show it last sold in 2009 for $520,000. Related Article Auctions ‘Most challenging market in 30 years’: Inner west vendors cut reserve to sell waterfront home The property had a reserve of $1.45 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Errichiello said it was evident there was “enthusiasm” from buyers hoping for a good price in current market conditions.



“If we had guided [this property] a bit lower, we would have had more people,” he said. “It [may be at a point where it’s] an uncomfortable price for vendors, but there are buyers to be had.” The property was one of 576 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Woolooware, a family from Dulwich Hill seeking to upsize from an apartment bid against themselves to secure the keys to a three-bedroom townhouse – a week after selling their own home. The property at 16/73 Denman Avenue had a guide of $1.4 million, which was also the opening bid. The bidders, the single registered party, then bid against themselves, initially going up to $1.42 million.



That was followed by two further bids of $5000 before the home sold under the hammer for $1.43 million. It had a reserve of $1.52 million. Sales agent for Pulse Property, Liam Farrell, said the family would not have been able to turn the sale around so quickly if it were not for the auction process. The two-storey townhouse has a covered outdoor area running off the open plan living area. Domain “They only sold [their property] last Saturday and came through [their new home] on Monday,” he said. “This time last year, we would have had five or six buyers, but today there was only one. If this was private treaty, this buyer would not have turned it around so quickly.”

World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions First home buyers pick up mid-century inner-north apartment for $752,000 Wes Mountain October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A two-bedroom, top-floor 1970s apartment in Carlton North sold for $752,000 at auction on Saturday, with three bidders pushing it almost $40,000 above its listed reserve. With a classic design featuring windows on three-sides, the light-filled mid-century home at 15/109 Wilson Street had been owned by the vendors as an investment for more than 35 years, and was listed as Carlton North but sits in the smaller, sought-after pocket of Princes Hill. As well as a separate bathroom, laundry and toilet, the property has two large bedrooms and an east-facing balcony off its long living room, and had a listed reserve of $715,000. Saturday marks the first weekend where all vendors were required to make their reserves public at least seven days before auction day.



Jellis Craig Fitzroy agent and auctioneer Charles Atkins said he thought the legislation had “brought more transparency to the marketplace” and was part of the reason the property had such a “solid campaign”, with competition between three active bidders on the day. Related Article NSW residential property Buyers love art deco apartments. These ‘no frills’ homes might be better He said a young couple opened the bidding at the $715,000 reserve, with bidding then going up in increments of $5000 and $1000 before it eventually sold to a couple who were first home buyers. The couple have a design background and were keen to make the home their own, Atkins said. “People enjoy that ’70s style block,” he said. “It has great natural light, big bones, great proportions. Terrific scope to add some value.”



The property was one of 466 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. With windows on three sides, typical of the era but rare in modern apartments, the property is well-lit throughout. Jellis Craig Fitzroy In Hampton, a contemporary four-bedroom townhouse sold for its listed $1.85 million reserve in post-auction negotiations, after passing in on a single genuine bid of $1.81 million. The property last sold in 2022 for $1.91 million. The home at 14A Field Street features open-plan living and dining areas looking out to a large rear yard through floor-to-ceiling windows, and a choice of two main bedrooms across the two levels, and a study nook, upstairs retreat and butler’s pantry.



Buxton Sandringham agent and auctioneer Richard Slade said the size and scope to live on either level had made the home attractive to both upsizers and downsizers. Related Article Auctions Meet the Melbourne home sellers who are already publishing their reserves “It was the north half of the two [townhouses], so from a natural light perspective, it was very well received,” he said. Slade opened the auction with a $1.8 million vendor bid, which was followed by the sole $1.81 million bid on which it passed in. He said two other parties had indicated they would be keen to negotiate post auction, but the high bidders, local downsizers, met the reserve and sealed the deal.



Slade said he thought the first weekend of listed reserves suggested vendors who had a realistic idea of what their property was worth would sell well. “It will hopefully help encourage buyers to pursue a property and do their final due diligence in that final week to auction,” he said. The vendors were selling as they have moved to Sydney.

World.title: Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs
World.content:
Investigation NationalNSWCity life Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs Max Maddison October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Herb Greedy Hall in Marrickville echoed with hissing and howling. Members of Marrickville FC – one of the largest community football clubs in Australia – had arrived in their hundreds for an annual general meeting in early December. It was an amazing turnout given only 15 people had attended the AGM 10 months earlier. The Marrickville Red Devils. Marrickville FC A faction of parents and coaches had become quietly, then vocally, concerned about the direction of the Red Devils, as the club is affectionately known. Together, they established Marrickville Community Voice, a group of members whom they hoped would be elected onto the club’s board. The club had transformed from a community organisation into a commercial enterprise where money was the primary issue, one parent involved alleged later. A notable shift in the culture was evident in the inclusion of bonus performance payments for some junior coaches in 2026, claimed two parents.



But after the breakaway faction’s plans became known, supporters of the club’s president Bill Drossos and the management committee rallied, turning out in force to stop what they alleged was an attempt to “overthrow the board”. The meeting ran for 80 minutes and, at times, had the decorum of a boxing match. It would rank among the more controversial days in the club’s 80-year history. Seven parents, former coaches and members spoke to this masthead as part of this story. All except one did so on the condition of anonymity to protect relationships. There were questions at the AGM about an alleged lack of transparency about the club’s finances, such as why the commercial terms of a five-a-side competition, run as a joint venture between Marrickville and a company owned by Drossos, appeared shrouded in secrecy? Aside from the question of finances, the crux of the disagreement was a dispute over the soul of a community football club. Who should a sporting club be run for? And how much should winning be valued in children’s sport?



It is a microcosm of the modern era: one where more is understood about the cost of prioritising results in children’s football over enjoyment, but where high-performance football squads have proliferated as intensely involved parents, living vicariously through their kids, have pushed them to succeed. Related Article Sports science Injuries, burnout, huge bills: Are pushy parents ruining children’s sport? Culture Tom Engesser, the former technical director of Marrickville FC, personified one of the competing philosophies of coaching children’s sport. “If something didn’t come off, I had heard him say, ‘Wow that was a really good idea; it may not have come off because your skills don’t match your thinking’,” says a mother who was involved in her son’s Red Devils side.



“It wasn’t about winning. He encouraged them to take risks.” According to coaches and parents at Marrickville FC, the technical director took a high-level view on coaching. In a game as chaotic and error-prone as children’s football, the obvious temptation is risk mitigation: playing direct and punting the ball long – hopefully to one or two strong, fast and gifted players who score all your goals. Engesser’s approach was different – encouraging players to play more like Spain; passing and controlling possession which invariably causes mistakes. The cost can be short-term results. But the upshot is the development of players, who become infinitely better as they learn by making mistakes. When coaches emphasise outcomes, the risk is young players become trapped in a mentality that success is a precondition of involvement. In contrast, Engesser wanted players to be better thinking footballers and enjoy the game for enjoyment’s sake.



He was constantly telling people the peak dropout period for boys in football was when they turned 14 – the age when they realised they wouldn’t make it professionally, the mother says. “Some parents thought he wasn’t focused enough on winning,” she says. “But he wanted to keep as many kids in the game as possible.” Then he was gone. A post on Marrickville FC’s Facebook account in June last year notified members that Engesser, who had recently finished coaching the club’s first grade side, had decided after 17 years at the club, he would step down “effective immediately”. The announcement generated an outpouring of support for Engesser. “A huge loss for our club and all our players, get him back ASAP before another club grabs him,” read one post underneath the Facebook post. Engesser declined to comment.



Not only did Engesser depart, but evidence of a new coaching philosophy emerged. Obtained by this masthead, a contract for junior selective development coaches for the most recent winter season stipulates bonus payments would be triggered by various successes: $250 for finishing first, $250 for semi-final qualification, and $500 for a grand final win. “Balance player improvement and development with an equal focus on team and match-based success culminating in semi-final qualifications and a grand final championship,” reads a key performance indicator in the contract. Marrickville FC managing director Georgina Kokokiris told this masthead that Engesser had left of his own accord, saying the club offered to expand his role and his departure had “absolutely nothing to do with coaching philosophy”.



She said a “very small percentage” of the club’s teams were coached by paid accredited coaches, and those agreements were commercial in confidence. There were “many aspects in these agreements”, and the club had the “right balance of individual development and support of our juniors”, Kokokiris said. Finances On the blustery first evening of last December, Adam Smith entered the AGM with a list of seemingly straightforward questions he believed the club’s leadership should answer about its finances. Adam Smith, a Marrickville FC parent and club member, asked the club for greater financial transparency. Jessica Hromas Smith – a club member and parent with no involvement in the Marrickville Community Voice – held two main concerns: the club’s qualified audit opinion, and the summer five-a-side competition, a commercial relationship between Marrickville FC and Sportzology, a sports uniform supplier owned by Drossos and his wife.



The 50-50 profit-sharing joint venture had grown rapidly since being established in 2018, to now include 250 teams. Drossos told the AGM that Sportzology had invested a “lot of money” to build and design the program, which included the naming rights, website and intellectual property. Moreover, the agreement was established before he joined the club and the contract had been renewed the previous year at “arm’s length”, he said. Yet, when Smith asked if the terms of the contract would be made available, or even the dollar amount Sportzology earned be made public, Drossos demurred, saying: “It’s a commercial arrangement.” In comments to this masthead, Smith said he was surprised his questions at the AGM about the accounts were taken as an attack on the club. “It has grown from a volunteer-run community club into a $1.8 million operation, mostly from families’ registration, with paid staff,” he said. “The governance hasn’t kept up with the money. “At that size, an arrangement with a company connected to the president should be set out in the accounts. There is no related party note in them at all.”



In comments to this masthead, Drossos said the club had thousands of members and only one had requested access to the information. “Marrickville FC have many agreements with related party organisations including former and current management committee members and copies of these agreements and arrangements as you would expect are commercial in confidence,” he said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Government grants The football club that used taxpayer grant for coach and player wages, wine and pub meals Kokokiris denied the club had not disclosed details of the arrangement with Sportzology, which she said had been “independently approved” by the current board. Drossos had brought a “wealth of experience, large fundraising, and additional revenue streams” to the club, she said. “This has allowed us to invest back into our club and its members including keeping our community registration fees as low as possible and not increasing those community registration fees for the past three years,” she said.



For the past six years, Drossos has been head of partnerships at the Macarthur FC, home to the Bulls, an A-League franchise based in south-western Sydney. When it came time for questions, an already tense meeting turned ugly. Supporters of the existing management committee alleged the Marrickville Community Voice “breached privacy” by obtaining a list of parents’ emails to send them information about their plans without their consent. As the meeting ticked over an hour, club legend Ron Royston was asked to deliver his verdict on the board’s performance. The 70-year club veteran, revelling in Marrickville FC’s 183 winter teams, proclaimed the already good club was only going to get better, but offered a warning. To see so many people at the meeting was “brilliant”, he said. “But I’m just hoping you’ve been here for the right bloody reason, not to disrupt this club.” Whether heeding Royston’s advice or not, the Marrickville Community Voice disbanded. Ten months later, Smith says he is still waiting for answers.

World.title: The ‘toxic’ legacy of former Agent Orange site looms over new planning permit
World.content:
NationalVictoriaProperty development The ‘toxic’ legacy of former Agent Orange site looms over new planning permit Angelica Snowden October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A decade-old fight over development of a Fawkner site where some of the toxic chemicals used to make Agent Orange were manufactured has reignited after a “retrospective” planning application by the owners. The former Nufarm site at 102 McBryde Street, in Melbourne’s outer north, has been the subject of resident concerns since the mid-1990s when a clay cap was laid across the site to stop residue chemicals spreading into soil and nearby land. The location of the former Nufarm factory in Fawkner. Eddie Jim Nufarm manufactured agricultural chemicals, including parts of – but never the whole product – Agent Orange, a weapon used by the US army during the Vietnam War to strip vegetation, between 1962 and 1971. Community groups lost their campaign in 2018 to stop the site from being redeveloped into warehouses despite arguing that works may disturb the cap and allow leftover toxic waste to leach out.



Now, an application has been made to Merri-bek Council to grant a permit for concrete slabs and shipping containers that were already installed on the land, which backs on to Merri Creek. Related Article Anger from Fawkner locals over toxic site poised for redevelopment The permit application has attracted 98 objections. One letter, seen by The Age, urged the council to refuse it because of “the documented history of significant contamination at this site and the potential risks associated with further development and disturbance of the land”. “I am particularly concerned about the integrity of the existing clay cap and whether any works already undertaken, or proposed as part of this application, could disturb or compromise the containment of contaminated material,” the letter read. “I am further concerned that works appear to have already been undertaken at the site without the required planning approval.



“Given the site’s contamination history, it is important that council establish precisely what works have occurred, when they occurred, whether contaminated soil or other potentially contaminated material was disturbed or removed, where any material was taken, and what environmental controls were in place at the time. “The fact that works may already have occurred should not diminish the level of scrutiny applied to the current application.” The application, by companies S&A Piccirillo Paving Pty Ltd and A&F Basile Paving Pty Ltd, asks the council to approve the “retrospective buildings and works” for storing machinery and vehicles. The former Nufarm site backs onto Merri Creek in Fawkner. Eddie Jim



The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal ruled in 2018 that the landowners could build two warehouses, as long as the clay cap was maintained. The decision said the industrial work “will not raise an unacceptable level of risk to the environment, the health of residents or site users”. A community meeting was held about the current proposal last month, with about 30 people attending. Merri-bek councillor Sue Bolton called the retrospective application “quite outrageous”. “I feel a highly contaminated site like this should not be managed by planning permits. They should be managed by the state government to ensure there is never any activity that would lead to [disturbance] of the clay cap.” A Merri-bek council spokesperson said the permit related to the “retrospective application [that] applies to works already completed at the site”.



“Council is aware of the site history, and is aware there is an environmental audit on the site. The environmental audit on the site has previously been considered by VCAT,” they said. “The application received 98 objections throughout the public notice period, which has now closed.” Residents are concerned concrete slabs and shipping containers have been placed in the former Nufarm site without approval. Eddie Jim Council officers were reviewing the information supplied with the application, which included a preliminary environmental site assessment, and were “considering all feedback”, the spokesperson said. According to the environmental site assessment, “the capping layer can be considered functionally intact”. Council officers will prepare a report for a decision in December.



Answering a mobile number for Angela Piccirillo, a female voice said: “I’m not interested in commenting on anything,” when contacted. Questions about the application were sent to an email address for Piccirillo Paving, and another address listed on the application forms. No response was received by deadline. Operators on the land of the Nufarm site did not respond to requests for comment. Eddie Jim Resident and community campaigner for Toxic Free Fawkner, Zainab, who requested her last name not be published, said she was “dumbfounded” that an environmental report produced in 1995 may still be factored into decision-making about the site. “The decision that council makes in the coming months will become part of the history of this site. I hope they are comfortable with how they will be remembered,” she said. “It’s been nearly 70 years since Nufarm came to Fawkner and the legacy of this toxic site began. Residents are still fighting to have their health and safety taken seriously.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The president, his beloved dogs and the pet psychic
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaPsychology The president, his beloved dogs and the pet psychic Jack Nicas October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Buenos Aires: At first, there was nothing unusual about Celia Melamed’s new client. His English mastiff was dying, so he hired her to read its mind. But when she met the man with the messy hair, he kept apologising for his casual outfit. “He told me, ‘Sorry for being dressed like this; I’m always in a suit on television’,” Melamed recalled. “I don’t have a television, so I had no idea what he was talking about.” The man was Javier Milei, at the time a TV pundit in Argentina known for railing against the government. The mastiff was Conan, soon to be Argentina’s most famous dog. And Melamed, by extension, was about to become the nation’s most well-known animal psychic. Celia Melamed says Javier Milei, pictured, hired her to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. Marcelo Dubini/Caras via The New York Times That is because, a few years later, Milei was elected Argentina’s president, and Conan was a symbol of his brash campaign, as well as the genetic model for the handful of clones that are now the nation’s first dogs.



But in that first encounter about a decade ago, Conan was on his deathbed, and Melamed said she was communicating with him via an energy she felt in her chest. She said she relayed Milei’s message that he was desperately trying to save the dog. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump spends America’s billions to save a friend in need Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “What I remember is that he felt better afterwards,” she said of Milei. “Few people have such an intense connection with their animals.” Melamed then became his dedicated pet psychic. He kept hiring her for the next two years, she said, including to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. They stopped working together a few years before Milei was elected president in 2023. Milei and his spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment. He has long made clear that he views his dogs as more than just pets. Milei, who is unmarried and childless, refers to them as his children, and his press secretary has admonished reporters who ask about the animals, saying it is equivalent to snooping into his family.



As a result, the dogs have become a central mystery of Milei’s presidency. Only one has been seen publicly since he was elected president, and there have been frequent rumours that others have died. When Milei suddenly fired much of the presidential residence’s staff last month, Argentine pundits speculated the move had something to do with his dogs, which he has said are kept in separate kennels there. It has even become common political fodder in Argentina that Milei seeks out his dogs for advice. A top foreign diplomat and a long-time friend of Milei’s, both of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said they have heard Milei say so. Celia Melamed charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times When asked by journalists about the claim, Milei has responded coyly, saying what happens in his house is private. “If he gives me advice, he’s a genius,” Milei said in 2023, referring to Conan. (Although Conan died in 2017, Milei has suggested that one of the clones is Conan’s reincarnation.) Asked whether she delivered a dog’s counsel to the future president, Melamed cited client privacy.



Milei was hardly her only client. After her work for him became public a few years ago, her waitlist ballooned to two months, she said. From her tiny Buenos Aires apartment draped in wind chimes and dream catchers, Melamed, 67, charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds to find out what is ailing the animals, where they are hiding or how they are doing in the afterlife. She says she needs merely a photo of an animal to perceive its emotions and thoughts, typically via sensations in her body. Loading “How does it work?” she said. “I don’t know. I only know that it works.” She represents what appears to be increasing global interest in the business of pet telepathy, notwithstanding an absence of scientific evidence.



While there are no reliable statistics on the industry, self-proclaimed animal communicators and their clients have proliferated on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram. Popular animal communicators on social media say business is booming. Related Article Protests A nationwide shutdown tests Milei’s tough medicine for Argentina ”When I started out, I was pretty much alone,” said Cindy Brody, a communicator from Woodstock, New York, who has been in the business for nearly 40 years. Interest took off several years ago, she said, and now her waitlist was nearly a month long. She holds up to 20 sessions a week, charging $US275 an hour. “It’s our time now,” she said. Clara Martín, an animal communicator from Madrid, said her clients were also multiplying, including a wild-animal sanctuary in South Africa and a man living with 23 cats in Japan. “People understand their animals have something to say,” she said. Melamed said she first noticed her powerful intuition as a child when she could predict correct answers in guessing games. But she never cultivated those abilities during a career in veterinary medicine and bacteriology. Then, in 2008, she read a book about communicating with animals and began taking courses.



Two years later, a horse she was working with stepped on her, but when she telepathically forgave it, she said her pain went away. “I realised there was something much deeper going on,” she said. Over two visits to her home, I watched Melamed work. (Since the COVID-19 pandemic, she has read animals’ minds remotely.) She looked at photos of cats and dogs, closed her eyes and, according to her, connected with the animals almost instantaneously. Stressed animals could make her body feel tense, she said, while lost pets had made her smell things that provided a clue to their whereabouts. “Sometimes what I feel is difficult to put into words,” she said. “I try to be as reliable as possible.” In one case, she said she asked a dog with persistent diarrhoea if it had a message for its owner. “‘Tell her that I’m not her grandmother’,” Melamed recalled the dog responding. The owner was stunned, she said, and admitted she had called the dog her grandmother’s name because of its gait, but would stop. “From that communication onwards, the dog stopped having bloody diarrhoea,” Melamed said. Clara Quattrucci, 65, said she began booking regular appointments with Melamed two years ago after she helped her cocker spaniel, Mia, recover from the emotional trauma of an attack from another dog. “It honestly blew my mind,” she said.



Dozens of people now advertised pet-psychic services in Buenos Aires, up from just a handful a decade ago, she said. That is in part thanks to Melamed. She estimates she has trained about 700 people in her pet-communication workshops. “We’re all capable,” she said. “The only thing that blocks us is our belief we can’t.” At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times She even taught the person she believes took her place working with Milei’s dogs: the president’s sister. Karina Milei, who is arguably Argentina’s second most powerful government official, showed innate talent in communicating with animals, Melamed said. She took Melamed’s weekend workshop around 2019, and then texted Melamed for months after for more guidance. Shortly after, she said, Javier Milei stopped hiring her.



Karina Milei did not respond to a request for comment. Melamed said she voted for Javier Milei and looks back fondly on their time together. After Conan died, she said Milei hired her to communicate with the dog’s genetic replicas. They were rambunctious puppies, anxious about their new home, she recalled. “They all have different personalities,” she said. “Even though they are all clones.” Milei, a libertarian economist, named four of the five clones after libertarian economists. The fifth he named Conan. It is that dog that Milei says is a reincarnation of his original pet, Melamed said, noting it immediately knew the layout of his house. “I think it’s very likely,” she said. When she communicated with that clone, she added, “there was a feeling of familiarity.” Her endorsement of the theory could mean a lot to Argentina’s president, who seemed to think highly of Melamed’s apparent powers. At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover.



“For Celia, TOTAL GENIUS OF THE UNIVERSE,” it said, “the being of light who helped me find the way.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Mexican men sentenced to 158 years in prison for murdering Australian brothers Gabriela Martinez Michael Koziol and October 17, 2026 — 1:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ensenada, Mexico: The three Mexican men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad have each been sentenced to 158 years in prison. A court in Ensenada announced the sentence on Friday (Mexico time), one week after the three men – Jesús Gerardo (also known as “El Kekas”), Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús – were found guilty. Debra Robinson outside court after three Mexican men were convicted of killing her sons Callum and Jake. AFP The men’s full names were not identified by the court for legal reasons. A translated statement from the attorney-general’s office said the men were each sentenced to 158 years and nine months in prison; 135 years for aggravated homicide; 10 years and 9 months for aggravated robbery involving violence; and 13 years for the violent theft of a vehicle.



The Robinson brothers’ parents attended every day of the trial and were present last week when the men were found guilty. Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson. Nine News Debra and Martin Robinson held hands as judge Raúl Hernández Arellano read out his verdict as it was translated by an aide. There was no jury. “Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad,” Martin Robinson said outside the court. “While no verdict can ever bring back our boys, or ease the heartbreak of losing them, we hope this outcome represents an important step towards justice and accountability.



“Callum and Jake had their whole lives ahead of them, filled with dreams, love and promise. We will forever carry their memory in our hearts … They will never be forgotten.” The Robinsons speak to the media after the verdict. AFP The Robinson brothers and Rhoad disappeared in late April 2024 while they were camping in a remote surfing spot in beachside Baja California. Their bodies, along with that of a local farmer, were found days later at the bottom of a well. They had been shot. The prosecution successfully argued that the three tourists were victims of a robbery that went awry. The court heard the victims begged for mercy before they were murdered, and that the killers later mocked their pleas. Gerardo’s then-girlfriend, Ari Gisell, is already serving a 20-year sentence for instigating the robbery that led to the murders. She gave evidence that Gerardo had confessed to the crime. “I f---ed up three gringos,” he told her.



Jake, 31, was a doctor who was due to start a job at a hospital in Geelong when he returned to Australia. Callum, 32, was a talented sportsman who had played lacrosse professionally in the US. He was living in San Diego. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold Will Weissert and Meg Kinnard October 17, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. November’s midterm elections will hinge in large part on Americans’ attitudes toward the cost of living, and the polls show the public giving the president poor marks for his handling of the economy. Bloomberg Trump personally signed the legislation just last month. Named after late South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, it had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling the war against Ukraine. Trump’s unexpected move comes a week after he stunningly said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia. A poll by the AP-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research published on October 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress on Election Day on November 3.



Graham died in July but had advocated for stricter US sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine. His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation – then changed his mind on Friday. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress. Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.



The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death – with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy. The president’s latest action also followed him announcing last week that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president as he condemned Volodymyr Zelenskyy for striking Russia’s diesel refineries. AP Photo/Nathan Howard Trump said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Trump’s decision to strike a deal with Putin on diesel on the world market has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike, who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine – without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.



The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centrepiece for Senator Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister, who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. Related Article Analysis

Trump diplomacy Trump promised to end the Russia-Ukraine war in a day. Now he’s funding it In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: A single bid secures keys to inner west home for $150,000 below reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions A single bid secures keys to inner west home for $150,000 below reserve Robyn Willis October 17, 2026 — 1:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A woman from Greenacre bought a home in Croydon Park for $150,000 less than the reserve with a single bid on Saturday, paying $1.3 million at auction. The woman was the only registered bidder for 16 Brighton Avenue and initially made an offer before the auction starting of $1.25 million for the well-presented two-bedroom semi, which was guided at $1.35 million. However, Rich & Oliva sales agent Marco Errichiello convinced her to raise the offer with a formal bid of $1.3 million and the property sold. “She said that was the maximum she could afford to spend with the current rate rises,” Errichiello said. “[The vendor] thought it was better to have a sale in these conditions rather than wait.”



The two-bedroom semi has retained many of its original features. Domain The vendor has held it as an investment. Records show it last sold in 2009 for $520,000. Related Article Auctions ‘Most challenging market in 30 years’: Inner west vendors cut reserve to sell waterfront home The property had a reserve of $1.45 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Errichiello said it was evident there was “enthusiasm” from buyers hoping for a good price in current market conditions.



“If we had guided [this property] a bit lower, we would have had more people,” he said. “It [may be at a point where it’s] an uncomfortable price for vendors, but there are buyers to be had.” The property was one of 576 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. In Woolooware, a family from Dulwich Hill seeking to upsize from an apartment bid against themselves to secure the keys to a three-bedroom townhouse – a week after selling their own home. The property at 16/73 Denman Avenue had a guide of $1.4 million, which was also the opening bid. The bidders, the single registered party, then bid against themselves, initially going up to $1.42 million.



That was followed by two further bids of $5000 before the home sold under the hammer for $1.43 million. It had a reserve of $1.52 million. Sales agent for Pulse Property, Liam Farrell, said the family would not have been able to turn the sale around so quickly if it were not for the auction process. The two-storey townhouse has a covered outdoor area running off the open plan living area. Domain “They only sold [their property] last Saturday and came through [their new home] on Monday,” he said. “This time last year, we would have had five or six buyers, but today there was only one. If this was private treaty, this buyer would not have turned it around so quickly.”

World.title: First home buyers pick up mid-century inner-north apartment for $752,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions First home buyers pick up mid-century inner-north apartment for $752,000 Wes Mountain October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A two-bedroom, top-floor 1970s apartment in Carlton North sold for $752,000 at auction on Saturday, with three bidders pushing it almost $40,000 above its listed reserve. With a classic design featuring windows on three-sides, the light-filled mid-century home at 15/109 Wilson Street had been owned by the vendors as an investment for more than 35 years, and was listed as Carlton North but sits in the smaller, sought-after pocket of Princes Hill. As well as a separate bathroom, laundry and toilet, the property has two large bedrooms and an east-facing balcony off its long living room, and had a listed reserve of $715,000. Saturday marks the first weekend where all vendors were required to make their reserves public at least seven days before auction day.



Jellis Craig Fitzroy agent and auctioneer Charles Atkins said he thought the legislation had “brought more transparency to the marketplace” and was part of the reason the property had such a “solid campaign”, with competition between three active bidders on the day. Related Article NSW residential property Buyers love art deco apartments. These ‘no frills’ homes might be better He said a young couple opened the bidding at the $715,000 reserve, with bidding then going up in increments of $5000 and $1000 before it eventually sold to a couple who were first home buyers. The couple have a design background and were keen to make the home their own, Atkins said. “People enjoy that ’70s style block,” he said. “It has great natural light, big bones, great proportions. Terrific scope to add some value.”



The property was one of 466 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. With windows on three sides, typical of the era but rare in modern apartments, the property is well-lit throughout. Jellis Craig Fitzroy In Hampton, a contemporary four-bedroom townhouse sold for its listed $1.85 million reserve in post-auction negotiations, after passing in on a single genuine bid of $1.81 million. The property last sold in 2022 for $1.91 million. The home at 14A Field Street features open-plan living and dining areas looking out to a large rear yard through floor-to-ceiling windows, and a choice of two main bedrooms across the two levels, and a study nook, upstairs retreat and butler’s pantry.



Buxton Sandringham agent and auctioneer Richard Slade said the size and scope to live on either level had made the home attractive to both upsizers and downsizers. Related Article Auctions Meet the Melbourne home sellers who are already publishing their reserves “It was the north half of the two [townhouses], so from a natural light perspective, it was very well received,” he said. Slade opened the auction with a $1.8 million vendor bid, which was followed by the sole $1.81 million bid on which it passed in. He said two other parties had indicated they would be keen to negotiate post auction, but the high bidders, local downsizers, met the reserve and sealed the deal.



Slade said he thought the first weekend of listed reserves suggested vendors who had a realistic idea of what their property was worth would sell well. “It will hopefully help encourage buyers to pursue a property and do their final due diligence in that final week to auction,” he said. The vendors were selling as they have moved to Sydney.

World.title: Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs
World.content:
Investigation NationalNSWCity life Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs Max Maddison October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Herb Greedy Hall in Marrickville echoed with hissing and howling. Members of Marrickville FC – one of the largest community football clubs in Australia – had arrived in their hundreds for an annual general meeting in early December. It was an amazing turnout given only 15 people had attended the AGM 10 months earlier. The Marrickville Red Devils. Marrickville FC A faction of parents and coaches had become quietly, then vocally, concerned about the direction of the Red Devils, as the club is affectionately known. Together, they established Marrickville Community Voice, a group of members whom they hoped would be elected onto the club’s board. The club had transformed from a community organisation into a commercial enterprise where money was the primary issue, one parent involved alleged later. A notable shift in the culture was evident in the inclusion of bonus performance payments for some junior coaches in 2026, claimed two parents.



But after the breakaway faction’s plans became known, supporters of the club’s president Bill Drossos and the management committee rallied, turning out in force to stop what they alleged was an attempt to “overthrow the board”. The meeting ran for 80 minutes and, at times, had the decorum of a boxing match. It would rank among the more controversial days in the club’s 80-year history. Seven parents, former coaches and members spoke to this masthead as part of this story. All except one did so on the condition of anonymity to protect relationships. There were questions at the AGM about an alleged lack of transparency about the club’s finances, such as why the commercial terms of a five-a-side competition, run as a joint venture between Marrickville and a company owned by Drossos, appeared shrouded in secrecy? Aside from the question of finances, the crux of the disagreement was a dispute over the soul of a community football club. Who should a sporting club be run for? And how much should winning be valued in children’s sport?



It is a microcosm of the modern era: one where more is understood about the cost of prioritising results in children’s football over enjoyment, but where high-performance football squads have proliferated as intensely involved parents, living vicariously through their kids, have pushed them to succeed. Related Article Sports science Injuries, burnout, huge bills: Are pushy parents ruining children’s sport? Culture Tom Engesser, the former technical director of Marrickville FC, personified one of the competing philosophies of coaching children’s sport. “If something didn’t come off, I had heard him say, ‘Wow that was a really good idea; it may not have come off because your skills don’t match your thinking’,” says a mother who was involved in her son’s Red Devils side.



“It wasn’t about winning. He encouraged them to take risks.” According to coaches and parents at Marrickville FC, the technical director took a high-level view on coaching. In a game as chaotic and error-prone as children’s football, the obvious temptation is risk mitigation: playing direct and punting the ball long – hopefully to one or two strong, fast and gifted players who score all your goals. Engesser’s approach was different – encouraging players to play more like Spain; passing and controlling possession which invariably causes mistakes. The cost can be short-term results. But the upshot is the development of players, who become infinitely better as they learn by making mistakes. When coaches emphasise outcomes, the risk is young players become trapped in a mentality that success is a precondition of involvement. In contrast, Engesser wanted players to be better thinking footballers and enjoy the game for enjoyment’s sake.



He was constantly telling people the peak dropout period for boys in football was when they turned 14 – the age when they realised they wouldn’t make it professionally, the mother says. “Some parents thought he wasn’t focused enough on winning,” she says. “But he wanted to keep as many kids in the game as possible.” Then he was gone. A post on Marrickville FC’s Facebook account in June last year notified members that Engesser, who had recently finished coaching the club’s first grade side, had decided after 17 years at the club, he would step down “effective immediately”. The announcement generated an outpouring of support for Engesser. “A huge loss for our club and all our players, get him back ASAP before another club grabs him,” read one post underneath the Facebook post. Engesser declined to comment.



Not only did Engesser depart, but evidence of a new coaching philosophy emerged. Obtained by this masthead, a contract for junior selective development coaches for the most recent winter season stipulates bonus payments would be triggered by various successes: $250 for finishing first, $250 for semi-final qualification, and $500 for a grand final win. “Balance player improvement and development with an equal focus on team and match-based success culminating in semi-final qualifications and a grand final championship,” reads a key performance indicator in the contract. Marrickville FC managing director Georgina Kokokiris told this masthead that Engesser had left of his own accord, saying the club offered to expand his role and his departure had “absolutely nothing to do with coaching philosophy”.



She said a “very small percentage” of the club’s teams were coached by paid accredited coaches, and those agreements were commercial in confidence. There were “many aspects in these agreements”, and the club had the “right balance of individual development and support of our juniors”, Kokokiris said. Finances On the blustery first evening of last December, Adam Smith entered the AGM with a list of seemingly straightforward questions he believed the club’s leadership should answer about its finances. Adam Smith, a Marrickville FC parent and club member, asked the club for greater financial transparency. Jessica Hromas Smith – a club member and parent with no involvement in the Marrickville Community Voice – held two main concerns: the club’s qualified audit opinion, and the summer five-a-side competition, a commercial relationship between Marrickville FC and Sportzology, a sports uniform supplier owned by Drossos and his wife.



The 50-50 profit-sharing joint venture had grown rapidly since being established in 2018, to now include 250 teams. Drossos told the AGM that Sportzology had invested a “lot of money” to build and design the program, which included the naming rights, website and intellectual property. Moreover, the agreement was established before he joined the club and the contract had been renewed the previous year at “arm’s length”, he said. Yet, when Smith asked if the terms of the contract would be made available, or even the dollar amount Sportzology earned be made public, Drossos demurred, saying: “It’s a commercial arrangement.” In comments to this masthead, Smith said he was surprised his questions at the AGM about the accounts were taken as an attack on the club. “It has grown from a volunteer-run community club into a $1.8 million operation, mostly from families’ registration, with paid staff,” he said. “The governance hasn’t kept up with the money. “At that size, an arrangement with a company connected to the president should be set out in the accounts. There is no related party note in them at all.”



In comments to this masthead, Drossos said the club had thousands of members and only one had requested access to the information. “Marrickville FC have many agreements with related party organisations including former and current management committee members and copies of these agreements and arrangements as you would expect are commercial in confidence,” he said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Government grants The football club that used taxpayer grant for coach and player wages, wine and pub meals Kokokiris denied the club had not disclosed details of the arrangement with Sportzology, which she said had been “independently approved” by the current board. Drossos had brought a “wealth of experience, large fundraising, and additional revenue streams” to the club, she said. “This has allowed us to invest back into our club and its members including keeping our community registration fees as low as possible and not increasing those community registration fees for the past three years,” she said.



For the past six years, Drossos has been head of partnerships at the Macarthur FC, home to the Bulls, an A-League franchise based in south-western Sydney. When it came time for questions, an already tense meeting turned ugly. Supporters of the existing management committee alleged the Marrickville Community Voice “breached privacy” by obtaining a list of parents’ emails to send them information about their plans without their consent. As the meeting ticked over an hour, club legend Ron Royston was asked to deliver his verdict on the board’s performance. The 70-year club veteran, revelling in Marrickville FC’s 183 winter teams, proclaimed the already good club was only going to get better, but offered a warning. To see so many people at the meeting was “brilliant”, he said. “But I’m just hoping you’ve been here for the right bloody reason, not to disrupt this club.” Whether heeding Royston’s advice or not, the Marrickville Community Voice disbanded. Ten months later, Smith says he is still waiting for answers.

World.title: The ‘toxic’ legacy of former Agent Orange site looms over new planning permit
World.content:
NationalVictoriaProperty development The ‘toxic’ legacy of former Agent Orange site looms over new planning permit Angelica Snowden October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A decade-old fight over development of a Fawkner site where some of the toxic chemicals used to make Agent Orange were manufactured has reignited after a “retrospective” planning application by the owners. The former Nufarm site at 102 McBryde Street, in Melbourne’s outer north, has been the subject of resident concerns since the mid-1990s when a clay cap was laid across the site to stop residue chemicals spreading into soil and nearby land. The location of the former Nufarm factory in Fawkner. Eddie Jim Nufarm manufactured agricultural chemicals, including parts of – but never the whole product – Agent Orange, a weapon used by the US army during the Vietnam War to strip vegetation, between 1962 and 1971. Community groups lost their campaign in 2018 to stop the site from being redeveloped into warehouses despite arguing that works may disturb the cap and allow leftover toxic waste to leach out.



Now, an application has been made to Merri-bek Council to grant a permit for concrete slabs and shipping containers that were already installed on the land, which backs on to Merri Creek. Related Article Anger from Fawkner locals over toxic site poised for redevelopment The permit application has attracted 98 objections. One letter, seen by The Age, urged the council to refuse it because of “the documented history of significant contamination at this site and the potential risks associated with further development and disturbance of the land”. “I am particularly concerned about the integrity of the existing clay cap and whether any works already undertaken, or proposed as part of this application, could disturb or compromise the containment of contaminated material,” the letter read. “I am further concerned that works appear to have already been undertaken at the site without the required planning approval.



“Given the site’s contamination history, it is important that council establish precisely what works have occurred, when they occurred, whether contaminated soil or other potentially contaminated material was disturbed or removed, where any material was taken, and what environmental controls were in place at the time. “The fact that works may already have occurred should not diminish the level of scrutiny applied to the current application.” The application, by companies S&A Piccirillo Paving Pty Ltd and A&F Basile Paving Pty Ltd, asks the council to approve the “retrospective buildings and works” for storing machinery and vehicles. The former Nufarm site backs onto Merri Creek in Fawkner. Eddie Jim



The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal ruled in 2018 that the landowners could build two warehouses, as long as the clay cap was maintained. The decision said the industrial work “will not raise an unacceptable level of risk to the environment, the health of residents or site users”. A community meeting was held about the current proposal last month, with about 30 people attending. Merri-bek councillor Sue Bolton called the retrospective application “quite outrageous”. “I feel a highly contaminated site like this should not be managed by planning permits. They should be managed by the state government to ensure there is never any activity that would lead to [disturbance] of the clay cap.” A Merri-bek council spokesperson said the permit related to the “retrospective application [that] applies to works already completed at the site”.



“Council is aware of the site history, and is aware there is an environmental audit on the site. The environmental audit on the site has previously been considered by VCAT,” they said. “The application received 98 objections throughout the public notice period, which has now closed.” Residents are concerned concrete slabs and shipping containers have been placed in the former Nufarm site without approval. Eddie Jim Council officers were reviewing the information supplied with the application, which included a preliminary environmental site assessment, and were “considering all feedback”, the spokesperson said. According to the environmental site assessment, “the capping layer can be considered functionally intact”. Council officers will prepare a report for a decision in December.



Answering a mobile number for Angela Piccirillo, a female voice said: “I’m not interested in commenting on anything,” when contacted. Questions about the application were sent to an email address for Piccirillo Paving, and another address listed on the application forms. No response was received by deadline. Operators on the land of the Nufarm site did not respond to requests for comment. Eddie Jim Resident and community campaigner for Toxic Free Fawkner, Zainab, who requested her last name not be published, said she was “dumbfounded” that an environmental report produced in 1995 may still be factored into decision-making about the site. “The decision that council makes in the coming months will become part of the history of this site. I hope they are comfortable with how they will be remembered,” she said. “It’s been nearly 70 years since Nufarm came to Fawkner and the legacy of this toxic site began. Residents are still fighting to have their health and safety taken seriously.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The president, his beloved dogs and the pet psychic
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaPsychology The president, his beloved dogs and the pet psychic Jack Nicas October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Buenos Aires: At first, there was nothing unusual about Celia Melamed’s new client. His English mastiff was dying, so he hired her to read its mind. But when she met the man with the messy hair, he kept apologising for his casual outfit. “He told me, ‘Sorry for being dressed like this; I’m always in a suit on television’,” Melamed recalled. “I don’t have a television, so I had no idea what he was talking about.” The man was Javier Milei, at the time a TV pundit in Argentina known for railing against the government. The mastiff was Conan, soon to be Argentina’s most famous dog. And Melamed, by extension, was about to become the nation’s most well-known animal psychic. Celia Melamed says Javier Milei, pictured, hired her to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. Marcelo Dubini/Caras via The New York Times That is because, a few years later, Milei was elected Argentina’s president, and Conan was a symbol of his brash campaign, as well as the genetic model for the handful of clones that are now the nation’s first dogs.



But in that first encounter about a decade ago, Conan was on his deathbed, and Melamed said she was communicating with him via an energy she felt in her chest. She said she relayed Milei’s message that he was desperately trying to save the dog. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump spends America’s billions to save a friend in need Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “What I remember is that he felt better afterwards,” she said of Milei. “Few people have such an intense connection with their animals.” Melamed then became his dedicated pet psychic. He kept hiring her for the next two years, she said, including to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. They stopped working together a few years before Milei was elected president in 2023. Milei and his spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment. He has long made clear that he views his dogs as more than just pets. Milei, who is unmarried and childless, refers to them as his children, and his press secretary has admonished reporters who ask about the animals, saying it is equivalent to snooping into his family.



As a result, the dogs have become a central mystery of Milei’s presidency. Only one has been seen publicly since he was elected president, and there have been frequent rumours that others have died. When Milei suddenly fired much of the presidential residence’s staff last month, Argentine pundits speculated the move had something to do with his dogs, which he has said are kept in separate kennels there. It has even become common political fodder in Argentina that Milei seeks out his dogs for advice. A top foreign diplomat and a long-time friend of Milei’s, both of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said they have heard Milei say so. Celia Melamed charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times When asked by journalists about the claim, Milei has responded coyly, saying what happens in his house is private. “If he gives me advice, he’s a genius,” Milei said in 2023, referring to Conan. (Although Conan died in 2017, Milei has suggested that one of the clones is Conan’s reincarnation.) Asked whether she delivered a dog’s counsel to the future president, Melamed cited client privacy.



Milei was hardly her only client. After her work for him became public a few years ago, her waitlist ballooned to two months, she said. From her tiny Buenos Aires apartment draped in wind chimes and dream catchers, Melamed, 67, charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds to find out what is ailing the animals, where they are hiding or how they are doing in the afterlife. She says she needs merely a photo of an animal to perceive its emotions and thoughts, typically via sensations in her body. Loading “How does it work?” she said. “I don’t know. I only know that it works.” She represents what appears to be increasing global interest in the business of pet telepathy, notwithstanding an absence of scientific evidence.



While there are no reliable statistics on the industry, self-proclaimed animal communicators and their clients have proliferated on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram. Popular animal communicators on social media say business is booming. Related Article Protests A nationwide shutdown tests Milei’s tough medicine for Argentina ”When I started out, I was pretty much alone,” said Cindy Brody, a communicator from Woodstock, New York, who has been in the business for nearly 40 years. Interest took off several years ago, she said, and now her waitlist was nearly a month long. She holds up to 20 sessions a week, charging $US275 an hour. “It’s our time now,” she said. Clara Martín, an animal communicator from Madrid, said her clients were also multiplying, including a wild-animal sanctuary in South Africa and a man living with 23 cats in Japan. “People understand their animals have something to say,” she said. Melamed said she first noticed her powerful intuition as a child when she could predict correct answers in guessing games. But she never cultivated those abilities during a career in veterinary medicine and bacteriology. Then, in 2008, she read a book about communicating with animals and began taking courses.



Two years later, a horse she was working with stepped on her, but when she telepathically forgave it, she said her pain went away. “I realised there was something much deeper going on,” she said. Over two visits to her home, I watched Melamed work. (Since the COVID-19 pandemic, she has read animals’ minds remotely.) She looked at photos of cats and dogs, closed her eyes and, according to her, connected with the animals almost instantaneously. Stressed animals could make her body feel tense, she said, while lost pets had made her smell things that provided a clue to their whereabouts. “Sometimes what I feel is difficult to put into words,” she said. “I try to be as reliable as possible.” In one case, she said she asked a dog with persistent diarrhoea if it had a message for its owner. “‘Tell her that I’m not her grandmother’,” Melamed recalled the dog responding. The owner was stunned, she said, and admitted she had called the dog her grandmother’s name because of its gait, but would stop. “From that communication onwards, the dog stopped having bloody diarrhoea,” Melamed said. Clara Quattrucci, 65, said she began booking regular appointments with Melamed two years ago after she helped her cocker spaniel, Mia, recover from the emotional trauma of an attack from another dog. “It honestly blew my mind,” she said.



Dozens of people now advertised pet-psychic services in Buenos Aires, up from just a handful a decade ago, she said. That is in part thanks to Melamed. She estimates she has trained about 700 people in her pet-communication workshops. “We’re all capable,” she said. “The only thing that blocks us is our belief we can’t.” At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times She even taught the person she believes took her place working with Milei’s dogs: the president’s sister. Karina Milei, who is arguably Argentina’s second most powerful government official, showed innate talent in communicating with animals, Melamed said. She took Melamed’s weekend workshop around 2019, and then texted Melamed for months after for more guidance. Shortly after, she said, Javier Milei stopped hiring her.



Karina Milei did not respond to a request for comment. Melamed said she voted for Javier Milei and looks back fondly on their time together. After Conan died, she said Milei hired her to communicate with the dog’s genetic replicas. They were rambunctious puppies, anxious about their new home, she recalled. “They all have different personalities,” she said. “Even though they are all clones.” Milei, a libertarian economist, named four of the five clones after libertarian economists. The fifth he named Conan. It is that dog that Milei says is a reincarnation of his original pet, Melamed said, noting it immediately knew the layout of his house. “I think it’s very likely,” she said. When she communicated with that clone, she added, “there was a feeling of familiarity.” Her endorsement of the theory could mean a lot to Argentina’s president, who seemed to think highly of Melamed’s apparent powers. At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover.



“For Celia, TOTAL GENIUS OF THE UNIVERSE,” it said, “the being of light who helped me find the way.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
